title: Friction: which way it pushes, when we want it, and why it makes heat

summary.text: A train engine as strong as four thousand horses can stand still on a wet hill, with its wheels spinning. The engine only turns the wheels. The force that moves the train forward is friction from the rail. Friction is a contact force between two surfaces, and it acts against sliding. So friction can slow a rolling marble or push a walker forward. It can also carry a steel bowl along on a moving cloth. Whenever surfaces do slide, friction turns movement into heat. Your child measures stopping distances and tests what makes a rubbed coin warmer. They also sort the friction we want from the friction we fight.
summary.art: A goods train on a wet hill track in the rain with its wheels spinning, and a small inset of a child's foot pushing a sheet of newspaper backward on a floor.

intro.hook: Stand up and take one slow step forward. As you step, which way does your back foot push on the floor: forward or backward? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: It is hard to tell just by stepping. In the first activity, Finger Walk, you test it with two fingers and a loose sheet of paper. Many books say that friction is the force that slows things down. That is only half of what friction does. In this unit you find out which way friction pushes, and how to work it out for anything. You also find out where the movement goes when friction stops a rolling marble, and why brakes get hot.
intro.art: A child taking one slow step across a tiled floor, looking down at the back foot, with a question mark beside the foot.

outcomes: By the end I can say why friction is a contact force, and draw it as an arrow.
By the end I can work out which way friction acts, even when it pushes a walker forward.
By the end I can run a fair stopping distance test with repeats, a mean and a chart.
By the end I can find useful and unwanted friction in one machine, and say how to change each.
By the end I can explain that friction makes heat, and that more force or more rubbing makes more.
By the end I can use energy to explain why a faster thing needs a much longer distance to stop.
By the end I can say how air resistance and water resistance are like friction, and how upthrust is different.
By the end I can say what scientists still do not know about friction.

terms.meaning: Friction is a force between two surfaces that touch. It acts against sliding, or against the sliding that would happen without it.
terms.example: Friction between your chappal and the road stops your foot sliding when you walk.
terms.art: A chappal on a road, with a small arrow along the road under the sole.

terms.meaning: A contact force is a force that acts only while two things touch. Friction, a push from your hand and the pull of a rope are contact forces.
terms.example: A carrom striker feels friction from the board only while the striker touches the board.
terms.art: A hand pushing a box, with the touching place circled.

terms.meaning: A non-contact force acts between things that do not touch. Gravity and the force of a magnet are non-contact forces.
terms.example: A mango falls from the tree because gravity pulls the mango down, though nothing touches the mango.
terms.art: A mango falling from a branch and a magnet pulling a pin across a gap.

terms.meaning: A force diagram is a simple drawing of one thing with an arrow for each force on it. Each arrow points the way that force acts. A bigger force gets a longer arrow.
terms.example: A sliding book gets three arrows. Gravity points down, the table's push points up, and friction points backward.
terms.art: A box drawn as a rectangle with three labelled arrows: gravity, the table's push and friction.

terms.meaning: Static friction is friction between two surfaces that are not sliding over each other. It grows to match a push, up to a limit.
terms.example: You push a heavy almirah gently and it stays still. Static friction is pushing back just as hard as you push.
terms.art: A child pushing a heavy steel almirah that does not move, with two equal arrows facing each other.

terms.meaning: Sliding friction is friction between two surfaces that are sliding over each other. It is usually a little smaller than the biggest static friction.
terms.example: A carrom coin sliding across the board slows down because of sliding friction.
terms.art: A carrom coin sliding across a board, with a short arrow pointing against its movement.

terms.meaning: Rolling resistance is the force that slows a rolling ball or wheel. Most of it comes from the surface and the wheel being squashed a little as they roll. It is usually far smaller than sliding friction.
terms.example: A marble rolls a long way on a hard floor and stops soon on a soft towel.
terms.art: A marble pressing a small dip into a towel as it rolls.

terms.meaning: Traction is friction that pushes a walker or a wheel forward. It happens when a foot or a wheel pushes backward on the ground without slipping. Every walking animal moves by traction, including us.
terms.example: On wet mud a wheel has little traction, so the wheel spins and the auto stays where it is.
terms.art: An auto wheel on a road with one arrow from the wheel pushing back on the road and one from the road pushing the wheel forward.

terms.meaning: A lubricant is something slippery put between two surfaces to make friction smaller. Oil, grease, soap, wax and talcum powder are lubricants.
terms.example: A drop of oil on a door hinge stops the squeak, because the metal parts slide on oil.
terms.art: A drop of oil falling from an oil can onto a door hinge.

terms.meaning: Kinetic energy is the energy a thing has because it is moving. A faster thing has more of it, and so does a heavier thing.
terms.example: A cycle at twice the speed has four times the kinetic energy.
terms.art: Two cyclists, one slow and one fast, with a small and a large energy bar above them.

terms.meaning: Thermal energy is the energy of the tiny particles of a thing as they jiggle. When a thing has more thermal energy, it is hotter. In everyday talk we call it heat.
terms.example: After you brake hard on a cycle, the wheel rim is warm. The cycle's kinetic energy became thermal energy.
terms.art: A cycle wheel rim and brake pad, with wavy heat lines rising from the place where they rub.

terms.meaning: Wear is the slow loss of material from a surface that rubs against another surface.
terms.example: The heel of an old chappal is thinner on one side, because the road has worn the rubber away.
terms.art: An old chappal seen from the side, with the heel worn thin at the back edge.

terms.meaning: Drag is the force from air or water that acts against a thing moving through it. Air resistance and water resistance are the two kinds of drag.
terms.example: You feel drag when you cycle fast, and when you wade through a pool.
terms.art: A cyclist leaning into the wind and a child wading through waist-deep water, each with an arrow pointing backward.

terms.meaning: A streamlined shape is smooth and narrow at the front, so air or water flows round it easily. A streamlined thing has less drag.
terms.example: A kingfisher's long, pointed beak is streamlined. She dives into water with hardly a splash.
terms.art: A kingfisher diving beak-first into a pond, with smooth flow lines round her body.

terms.meaning: Upthrust is the upward push of water or air on a thing that is in it. Upthrust acts even when the thing is still. It is a contact force, but it is not a kind of friction.
terms.example: Push an empty bottle down into a bucket of water. The push you feel against your hand is upthrust.
terms.art: A hand pushing a closed empty bottle down into a bucket of water, with an arrow pointing up from the bottle.

terms.meaning: Stopping distance is how far a moving thing travels before it stops.
terms.example: A cycle going fast has a longer stopping distance than a cycle going slowly.
terms.art: A cycle with a dotted line on the road from where the rider brakes to where the cycle stops.

terms.meaning: The mean is one number that stands for several measurements. Add the measurements and divide by how many there are. It is also called the average.
terms.example: Three runs of 22, 26 and 24 centimetres add up to 72. The mean is 72 divided by 3, which is 24 centimetres.
terms.art: A notebook with three numbers added up and divided by three.

explanations.definition: Friction is a force between two surfaces that touch. It is a contact force, so it stops acting as soon as the surfaces part.
explanations.description: Forces come in two kinds. Contact forces need touching: a push from a hand, the pull of a rope, friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust. Non-contact forces act across a gap: gravity and the forces of magnets and electric charge. Friction acts along the surfaces, where they meet. In a force diagram we draw friction as an arrow lying along the surface. Friction depends on both surfaces, never on one alone. The same chappal grips a dry road well and a wet marble floor badly.
examples: A sliding carrom coin slows down on the board. Flick the coin off the edge, and that friction ends at once.
Gravity pulls a falling mango with nothing touching the mango. Friction cannot do that.
In a force diagram of a sliding book, the friction arrow lies along the table top and points backward.
explanations.art: A carrom coin on a board with an arrow along the board, beside a falling mango with an arrow pointing down through empty air.

explanations.definition: Friction acts along the touching surfaces. On each surface it points against the way that surface is sliding over the other, or would slide without friction.
explanations.description: To find the direction, ask one question. Which way is this surface sliding over the other one, or trying to slide? Friction on it points the opposite way. A book sliding to the right on a table gets friction to the left. A book resting on a tilted board would slide down, so friction on the book points up the slope. Friction always acts on both surfaces, as a pair of pushes. The table pushes the sliding book to the left. The book pushes the table to the right, just as hard. We seldom notice the second push, because the table is held by the floor.
examples: A child going down a slide moves down the slope, so friction on the child points up the slope.
Press a book against a wall with a flat hand. The book would slide down, so friction from the wall points up.
In Finger Walk, your fingers pushed the loose paper backward, and the paper slid backward. The paper's friction on your fingers pointed forward.
explanations.art: Three small drawings with friction arrows: a book sliding on a table, a book resting on a tilted board, and a book pressed against a wall.

explanations.definition: Traction is friction that pushes a walker or a wheel forward. Friction can also carry a thing along on a moving surface.
explanations.description: When you step forward, your back foot pushes backward on the floor. Without friction the foot would slide backward. So friction on your foot points forward, and that push moves you. A wheel does the same. The engine turns the wheel. The bottom of the wheel pushes backward on the road, and the road pushes the wheel forward. On ice, mud or wet rails the wheel slides and spins, and the vehicle stays where it is. Friction also carries things. Pull a cloth slowly and a steel bowl standing on the cloth moves with it. Only the cloth touches the bowl, so friction from the cloth moved the bowl. In every case friction acts to stop two touching surfaces sliding over each other.
examples: In the Riding Katori, a small steel bowl on a cloth moved when the cloth was pulled slowly. Friction speeded the bowl up.
A train carries dry sand. On wet rails the loco pilot blows sand under the wheels, so the wheels grip the rails again.
A snake's belly scales grip the ground more when they slide backward than forward. She pushes back on the ground and friction moves her forward.
A box on the back of a lorry speeds up with the lorry. Friction from the lorry's floor pushes the box forward.
explanations.art: A walker's back foot with one arrow from the foot pushing back on the floor and one arrow from the floor pushing the foot forward.

explanations.concept: Static friction: friction when nothing slides
explanations.definition: Static friction is friction between surfaces that are not sliding. It grows to match the push on a thing, up to a limit.
explanations.description: Push a heavy almirah gently and it does not move. Static friction pushes back exactly as hard as you push, so the two forces are balanced. Push harder and static friction grows too. But it has a limit. Past that limit the almirah starts to slide, and sliding friction takes over. Sliding friction is usually a little smaller, so the almirah feels easier once it moves. Walking and driving use static friction, because a sole or a tyre that grips does not slide. That is why a spinning wheel grips less than a wheel that is just holding.
examples: A book resting on a tilted board stays put. Static friction up the slope balances the part of gravity that pulls the book down the slope.
A knot stays tied because static friction stops the string sliding over itself.
A driver on a wet road brakes gently, so the tyres keep gripping and do not skid.
explanations.art: A child pushing an almirah with a small push arrow and an equal friction arrow, then a bigger push with a bigger friction arrow.

explanations.definition: Useful friction is friction that stops a slide we do not want. Unwanted friction is friction that works against a slide we do want. It is the same force both times.
explanations.description: One bicycle has both. We want the tyres to grip the road and the brake pads to grip the rim. We want the shoes to grip the pedals. We do not want friction in the axles or between the links of the chain. There it wastes the rider's effort as heat. To make friction bigger, people use rubber, rough surfaces, tread, a harder press, sand, or chalk on the hands. To make friction smaller, people use oil, grease, polished surfaces, wheels, ball bearings or a cushion of air. No surface is good or bad by itself. A smooth floor is right for dancing and wrong for a wet bathroom.
examples: Weightlifters and rock climbers rub chalk on their hands. Chalk soaks up sweat, so the hands grip better.
A carrom board is dusted with fine powder, so the coins slide further.
A screw holds two pieces of wood because of friction on its thread. With no friction, every screw and nut would work loose.
On a cycle, the brake pads need friction and the axle next to them needs oil.
explanations.art: A bicycle with green marks on the tyres, brake pads, pedals and handle grips, and red marks on the axles and the chain.

explanations.definition: When surfaces slide, friction turns kinetic energy into thermal energy. The energy changed is the friction force multiplied by the distance of sliding.
explanations.description: Energy is never destroyed. A moving thing has kinetic energy, and friction changes that energy into thermal energy in both surfaces. So a bigger friction force makes more heat, and a longer rub makes more heat. The same idea explains why things stop. A soft towel pushes hard against a rolling marble, so all the marble's energy is changed to heat in a short distance. A bedsheet pushes less hard. So the same energy lasts for a longer distance before the marble stops. A marble that starts twice as high has twice the energy, so it rolls about twice as far. Speed matters even more. Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy. So a cycle or a car at twice the speed needs about four times the distance to brake.
examples: In the Stopping Distance Test, the marble started at the 10 and the 20 centimetre marks. From 20 it rolled about twice as far.
In the Warm Coin Test, 80 strokes warmed the coin more than 20 strokes. A firm press warmed it more than a light press.
A cycle rim feels warm after hard braking down a slope. The cycle's kinetic energy is now heat in the rim and the pads.
A lorry coming down a long ghat road uses a low gear, so that the brakes do not overheat.
explanations.art: A cycle braking, with a large kinetic energy bar shrinking and a thermal energy bar growing at the brake pads.

explanations.definition: Heat is the jiggling of the atoms and molecules of a thing. Sliding surfaces tug on each other's atoms and let go, and that sets the atoms jiggling faster.
explanations.description: Two surfaces really touch only at many tiny spots. At each spot the atoms of one surface hold on to the atoms of the other. As the surfaces slide, each spot is stretched, and then the atoms snap free. They are left shaking, like a plucked string. That shaking is thermal energy. It spreads from atom to atom into the rest of each surface, and then into the air. This only goes one way. Once the shaking has spread out, it does not gather again and push the surfaces back to where they started. Scientists agree on this much. They are still working out the details. One is how much of the energy goes first into atoms, and how much into electrons.
examples: Rub your palms together for ten seconds and they are warm.
A match lights because friction heats one tiny spot on the match head enough to start the chemicals burning.
A drill bit is too hot to touch after it has made a hole in a wall.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of two rough surfaces touching at a few peaks, with the atoms at the peaks drawn shaking.

explanations.definition: Wear is the loss of tiny pieces from surfaces that rub. Every sliding contact causes some wear.
explanations.description: At the tiny spots where two surfaces touch, sliding can tear small pieces off. Usually the softer surface loses more. Sometimes we want wear. A pencil writes because friction pulls thin flakes of graphite off the tip and leaves them on the paper. An eraser works because the rubber grips those flakes and wears away into crumbs that carry them off. More often wear is a cost. Brake pads, tyres, shoe soles and the parts of engines all wear out and must be replaced. Oil helps twice. It makes friction smaller, and it keeps the surfaces apart so they wear more slowly.
examples: The steps of an old temple or railway station dip in the middle. Millions of feet have worn the stone away.
A cycle's brake pads become thinner every month.
The dust from worn tyres is washed off roads by the rain and ends up in rivers and the sea.
explanations.art: Old stone steps worn into a dip in the middle, with a new square step drawn beside them for comparison.

explanations.definition: Air resistance and water resistance are forces from air and water that act against a thing moving through them. Together they are called drag.
explanations.description: Drag is like friction in three ways. It is a contact force, it acts against the movement, and it turns kinetic energy into heat. It is also different. Friction between two solid surfaces changes little with speed. Drag, however, grows fast as speed grows. Drag also depends on shape and on how big a front the thing pushes through the air or water. A streamlined shape has less drag. Upthrust is a different force. It is the upward push of water or air on a thing that is in it. Upthrust acts even on a thing that is still, and it points up, not against the movement. A boat floats because upthrust balances gravity. The boat slows down because of water resistance.
examples: Sweep a flat hand through a bucket of water, then a hand held edge-on. The flat hand is much harder to move. You try this in Hand in the Bucket.
Racing cyclists crouch low, so they push a smaller front through the air.
An empty bottle pushed under water pushes back up on your hand even when you hold it still. That is upthrust, not water resistance.
explanations.art: A swimmer gliding with a drag arrow pointing backward, and a floating boat with an upthrust arrow pointing up and a gravity arrow pointing down.

explanations.definition: Rolling resistance is the force that slows a rolling ball or wheel. People disagree about whether to call it friction.
explanations.description: A rolling marble does not slide over the towel, so the usual cause of friction is missing. Yet something slows the marble. As the marble rolls, it presses a small dip into the cloth, and the cloth springs back behind it. The fibres bend and rub against each other, and that takes energy from the marble and turns it into heat. A hard floor is squashed far less, so a marble rolls much further on it. Whatever name we use, the force acts where two things touch, it acts against the movement, and it makes heat.
examples: A cycle with soft tyres is harder to pedal, because the soft tyres squash more as they roll.
A steel train wheel on a steel rail squashes very little. That is one reason a train needs so little energy for each tonne it carries.
In the Stopping Distance Test, the marble stopped sooner on a soft towel than on a thin bedsheet.

perspectives.explanation: They call it friction. It acts between two touching surfaces and against the movement, and that is what friction means at this level.
They call it rolling resistance and keep it apart from friction. It comes mostly from squashing and springing back, not from surfaces sliding.

explanations.art: A marble on a towel with the towel squashed into a dip under the marble, and the same marble on a hard tile with no dip.

agreed.text: Friction acts only where two surfaces touch, and it acts against sliding between them.
agreed.evidence: Thousands of pull and slope tests show this, from Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks more than 500 years ago to laboratories today.

agreed.text: Friction acts on both surfaces at once, with equal forces in opposite directions.
agreed.evidence: This is Newton's third law, published in 1687. You can see it when loose paper slides backward under walking fingers.

agreed.text: Walkers and wheels move forward because of friction from the ground.
agreed.evidence: On ice, wet mud or oily rails, feet slip and wheels spin. Railway engines carry sand to put grip back on wet rails.

agreed.text: Friction turns kinetic energy into heat, and no energy is lost on the way.
agreed.evidence: In the 1840s James Joule stirred water with paddles turned by falling weights. The same amount of work always gave the same amount of heat.

agreed.text: A vehicle at twice the speed needs about four times the distance once the brakes are on.
agreed.evidence: Kinetic energy grows with the speed multiplied by itself. Road tests of braking cars agree with this.

agreed.text: Drag from air and water grows quickly with speed and depends on shape.
agreed.evidence: Engineers measure drag on models of cars, planes and ships in wind tunnels and water tanks.

challenging.claim: Friction always acts against the way a thing is moving.
challenging.for: It is true for a sliding box, a rolling ball and a braking cycle. These are the examples most books use.
challenging.against: Friction on a walker's foot points forward, the way the walker moves. So does friction on a steel bowl carried along by a pulled cloth. The full rule is that friction acts against sliding between two surfaces.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule in many books: that friction always points against the movement.

challenging.claim: The energy that friction takes from a moving thing is lost for ever.
challenging.for: A cyclist who brakes cannot get her speed back from the warm brake pads. For her, that energy is gone.
challenging.against: The energy still exists as heat. James Joule showed in the 1840s that work always turns into a fixed amount of heat. The heat only spreads out, so it is hard to use again.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens to the energy of a moving thing when friction stops it.

challenging.claim: A vehicle can be stopped without turning all its movement into heat.
challenging.who: Engineers of electric trains and cars
challenging.for: In regenerative braking the turning wheels drive the motors backward, and the motors make electricity. Delhi Metro trains feed braking energy back into the overhead wires.
challenging.against: Some energy still becomes heat. Every train and car also keeps ordinary friction brakes for the last few metres and for emergencies.
challenging.context: This card is about braking that saves energy and does not waste all of it as heat.

challenging.claim: A heavier vehicle always needs a longer distance to brake.
challenging.for: A heavier vehicle has more kinetic energy at the same speed. Loaded lorries really do take longer to stop, because their brakes and tyres reach their limits.
challenging.against: More weight also presses the tyres harder on the road, so the friction grows by about the same share. In simple tests, a heavy and a light sliding block stop in about the same distance.
challenging.context: This card is about whether weight changes how far a braking vehicle travels.

challenging.claim: A world with no friction would be a better world for machines.
challenging.for: One study in 2017 estimated that about one fifth of the energy the world uses is spent on overcoming friction. Worn parts cost a great deal to replace.
challenging.against: With no friction, no wheel could push on a road and no brake could work. No screw, nut or knot would stay tight. Engineers aim for the right friction in each place, not for none.
challenging.context: This card is about whether machines would be better with no friction at all.

big_questions.q: The floor pushes you forward at every step. So when you walk, who moves you: your legs, or the floor?
big_questions.hint: Try the newspaper under your foot again. What do your legs do, and what does the floor do?

big_questions.q: The same force is useful on a brake and unwanted in an axle. Is 'useful' a fact about friction, or about us?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is doing the wanting in each case.

big_questions.q: Friction needs two surfaces. Does a chappal by itself have any grip?
big_questions.hint: Think of the same chappal on a dry road and on a wet marble floor.

big_questions.q: When a marble stops, its energy has become heat that spreads into the room. Could that heat ever start the marble rolling again?
big_questions.hint: Have you ever seen a still marble start to roll because the room was warm?

big_questions.q: About one fifth of the world's energy goes on overcoming friction. Whose job is it to waste less of it?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cyclist who oils a chain, a driver, an engineer and a government.

big_questions.q: Tyres and brakes wear into dust that ends up in rivers and the sea. Is the friction we use on roads free?
big_questions.hint: Somebody, somewhere, breathes or drinks what is rubbed off.

story.title: A Handful of Sand
story.note: A made-up story. The science and the railway are real. The Braganza Ghat runs between Kulem in Goa and Castle Rock in Karnataka. It is a very steep railway climb. Trains usually climb it with two engines in front and one pushing at the back, and the Dudhsagar waterfall falls beside the track. Indian engines carry sand to drop on slippery rails. Yazhini, Shanta Chithi, the passengers and this journey are imagined.
text: The train left Kulem station in the rain. It was July, and Yazhini was ten. She sat with her nose against the window bars, because somewhere up this hill was the Dudhsagar waterfall.
Her aunt, Shanta Chithi, sat across from her with a steel tiffin box on her knees. Chithi drove goods trains for the railway. Today she was only a passenger, going home to Hubballi on leave.

The hill ahead was called the Braganza Ghat. For twenty-six kilometres the track climbed through wet forest. It was a very steep railway climb. At Kulem the railway had joined one more engine to the back of the train, to push.
"How many engines do we have?" Yazhini asked.
"Three. Two in front and one pushing from behind," said Chithi. "Each one is as strong as about four thousand horses."

Yazhini tried to picture twelve thousand horses. She could not. The train climbed slowly, through one tunnel and then another. Rain ran down the bars. Wet leaves lay stuck to the sleepers, and on the shining tops of the rails.
Then the forest opened, and there was the waterfall. White water came down the whole height of the mountain, so close that spray blew in through the window. Everyone in the coach stood up to look.

The train slowed. It slowed some more. Then a sound came from the front of the train, a rising whirr, like a mixer running with nothing in the jar. The coach shook. Outside, the trees stood perfectly still.
"We have stopped," said a man by the door. "Three engines, and they are still too weak for this rain. They should have sent a bigger one."
"The train is too heavy," said a woman with a basket of bananas. "Half of us should get down and walk."

Yazhini listened to the whirr. It reminded her of something. That morning she had run across her grandmother's wet veranda in her socks, to catch the auto. Her legs had gone very fast. She had gone nowhere at all. Then she had sat down hard on the red floor.
My legs were not weak, she thought. My legs were working. The floor was not holding my feet.

"Chithi," she said slowly, "I don't think the engines are weak. I can hear the wheels turning. They are turning, and the train is standing still. So the wheels are slipping on the rails, like my socks on Paati's veranda."
Chithi put the lid back on her tiffin box. "Go on," she said.

"An engine only turns its wheels," said Yazhini. "The wheel pushes backward on the rail. If the rail holds the wheel, the rail pushes the train forward. But the rail is wet, and there are leaves on it. So the wheel just slides round. Nothing is pushing us."
"And if you were the loco pilot?" asked Chithi. "Would you ask for a fourth engine?"
Yazhini shook her head. "A fourth engine would spin too. I would not make the wheels stronger. I would make the rail hold them. I would put something rough under the wheels."
Chithi smiled. "Listen," she said.
The whirr had dropped to a low growl. Then from the front came a long hiss of air.

"First the pilot lowers the power," said Chithi. "A wheel that is spinning grips even less than a wheel that is holding. Then she presses the sand button. Every engine carries boxes of dry sand. Air blows the sand down a pipe, onto the rail, just in front of the wheel."
The coach gave a small jerk. A tree trunk slid past the window, then another. The waterfall began to move away behind them.
"There," said the man by the door. "They have switched on more power at last."
"Less," said Yazhini, but only Chithi heard her.

At the top of the ghat the train stopped at Castle Rock, and the pushing engine was taken off. Yazhini climbed down and walked along the wet platform to the front. She bent to look at the place where a great steel wheel stood on the rail.
The wheel was more than a metre across. But the place where it touched the rail was tiny, smaller than a one-rupee coin. On the rail beside it lay a little pale dust, the last of the crushed sand.
"All those horses," she said, "and they push through a patch that size."
"Twelve thousand horses," said Chithi, "and a handful of sand."
Yazhini walked back along the platform. It was wet, so she walked carefully. At each step she felt her sandal press backward on the stone, and the stone push her on.
story.epiphany: For the parent: an engine does not push a train. The engine turns the wheels, and the wheels push backward on the rails. Friction from the rails pushes the train forward. This forward friction is called traction. On wet, leafy rails the friction is too small, so the wheels spin and all the engine's power does nothing. More power makes it worse, because a spinning wheel grips less than a wheel that is holding. Sand makes the friction bigger, and the train moves. The same thing happens under a shoe at every step.
ask: The engines were working, yet the train stood still. What was missing?
Why did Yazhini think of her socks on the wet veranda?
Which way does the wheel push on the rail? Which way does the rail push on the wheel?
Why did the loco pilot lower the power before she used the sand?
Where else have you seen a wheel or a foot slip? What gave back the grip?

games.context: This is a card game about the direction of friction. Each card describes one thing. You point a paper arrow the way friction pushes on that thing, then turn the card to check.
