items.f: A carrom coin slides across the board to the right. Which way does friction push the coin?
items.b: To the left. The coin slides to the right over the board, and friction acts against that slide.

items.f: A girl starts to walk forward. Which way does friction from the floor push her back foot?
items.b: Forward. Her foot pushes backward on the floor. Friction stops the foot sliding back, so it points forward.

items.f: A cycle is braking on a road. Which way does friction from the road push the tyres?
items.b: Backward. The braked tyres try to slide forward over the road, and friction acts against that.

items.f: A book rests on a tilted desk and does not slide. Which way does friction push the book?
items.b: Up the slope. Without friction the book would slide down the slope.

items.f: A steel bowl stands on a cloth. The cloth is pulled slowly to the left, and the bowl rides along. Which way does friction push the bowl?
items.b: To the left. Friction from the cloth carries the bowl along, the same way it moves.

items.f: A suitcase rides on a level airport belt at a steady speed. How much friction pushes the suitcase along?
items.b: None. The suitcase and the belt move together at a steady speed, so nothing is trying to slide.

items.f: An airport belt starts up with a suitcase lying on it. Which way does friction push the suitcase?
items.b: Forward, the way the belt moves. Friction speeds the suitcase up until it moves with the belt.

items.f: A lorry speeds up, with a box on its flat back. The box does not slide. Which way does friction push the box?
items.b: Forward. Without friction the box would be left behind and slide off the back.

items.f: A lorry brakes, with a box on its flat back. The box does not slide. Which way does friction push the box?
items.b: Backward. Without friction the box would keep going and slide towards the driver's cabin.

items.f: A child goes down a playground slide. Which way does friction push the child?
items.b: Up the slide. The child slides down, and friction acts against that slide.

items.f: You press a book against a wall with a flat hand, and the book stays up. Which way does friction from the wall push the book?
items.b: Up. Gravity would slide the book down the wall, and friction acts against that.

items.f: A car speeds up. The engine turns the front wheels. Which way does friction from the road push those tyres?
items.b: Forward. The bottom of each tyre pushes backward on the road, so the road's friction pushes the tyre forward.

items.f: A football rolls across grass and slows down. Which way does the grass push the ball?
items.b: Backward. The grass bends and rubs under the ball, and that force acts against the rolling.

items.f: You push a heavy almirah gently to the right, and it does not move. Which way does friction push the almirah?
items.b: To the left, exactly as hard as your push. This is static friction.

items.f: A climber grips a rope with both hands and hangs still. Which way does friction from the rope push her hands?
items.b: Up. Gravity would slide her hands down the rope, and friction acts against that.

items.f: A train tries to start on wet rails, and its wheels spin. Which way does friction from the rail push the wheels?
items.b: Forward, but too weakly. The bottom of each wheel slides backward over the rail, so friction points forward.

items.f: A match head is dragged to the right along the side of the box. Which way does friction push the match head?
items.b: To the left. That friction also heats the match head until it lights.

items.f: A swimmer pushes off the wall and glides forward. Which way does water resistance push her?
items.b: Backward. Water resistance acts against her movement through the water.

items.f: A girl cycles fast through still air. Which way does air resistance push her?
items.b: Backward. Air resistance acts against her movement through the air.

items.f: A box stands on a level floor, and nobody pushes it. How much friction acts on the box?
items.b: None. Nothing is trying to slide the box, so static friction has nothing to match.

printables.title: A paper arrow for each player

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up. Each player takes a paper arrow.
One player reads the top card aloud and shows with a hand which way the thing is moving.
On the count of three, every player lays down their arrow to show the way friction pushes. For 'none', keep the arrow in your hand.
Turn the card over. Every player who was right and can give the reason scores one point.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score one point for each card you get right. Try to reach 16 out of 20, then play again.

setup.art: A pile of question cards on a table and a paper arrow in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile. Each player takes a paper arrow.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while moving one hand to the right to show a sliding carrom coin.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card and show which way the thing moves.

setup.art: Two paper arrows laid on the table, both pointing left, and the card turned over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Lay down your arrow, then turn the card to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and the arrows. 2. Shuffle the cards. 3. Put them in a pile, question side up.
flow.say: Each card describes one thing. We will work out which way friction pushes on that thing. Sometimes the answer is a surprise.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the arrows. Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Way Is the Friction? Here you set up the cards and the paper arrows.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone lays down an arrow. 4. Turn the card over and read the reason.
flow.say: Ask yourself one question. Which way would this thing slide if there were no friction? Friction pushes the other way.
flow.kid: Read the card. Which way would it slide with no friction? Point your arrow the other way.

ask.q: A lorry speeds up with a box on its back. Why does friction on the box point forward?
good: Without friction the box would be left behind and slide backward.
Friction acts against that slide, so it points forward.

flow.parent: The useful question is always the same: which way would it slide with no friction? If your child points against the movement every time, ask that question again for the walker and the lorry cards.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Way Is the Friction? Here you read each card and show the direction of friction with an arrow.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the cards that anyone got wrong. 3. Sort all 20 cards into two heaps: friction against the movement, and friction with the movement or none.
flow.say: Which cards surprised us? In which ones did friction point the same way as the movement?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which cards surprised you? Sort the cards into two heaps.

check.q: A girl starts to walk forward. Which way does friction from the floor push her back foot?
options: Backward, because friction always slows things
Forward, because her foot pushes backward on the floor
Downward, into the floor
check.why: Her foot pushes backward on the floor and would slide backward without friction. So friction on the foot points forward. Choosing 'backward' usually means using the rule 'friction is against the movement'. The full rule is that friction is against sliding.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Way Is the Friction? Here you count the points and sort the cards.

games.title: Shove Coin: stop on the line
games.context: This is a sliding game. You shove a coin along a smooth table and try to stop it on a line 60 centimetres away. Then you change the friction with powder or a cloth, and play again.

printables.title: The target, drawn with pencil or chalk on the table
items: Start line: at the near edge of the table
Target line: 60 centimetres from the start line
3 points: the coin stops touching the target line
2 points: the coin stops within one hand-width of the line
1 point: the coin stops within two hand-widths of the line
0 points: the coin stops further away, or falls off the table

printables.title: Score sheet for three rounds
items: Round 1, bare table: five shoves each. Points: __
Round 2, table dusted with powder: five shoves each. Points: __
Round 3, on a bedsheet: five shoves each. Points: __
Which round needed the hardest shove? __
Which round needed the gentlest shove? __

rules: Mark a start line and a target line 60 centimetres apart on a smooth table. Use a pencil, chalk or strips of paper tape.
Put a coin on the start line. Shove it once with one finger, in one quick push.
Score 3, 2, 1 or 0 by where the coin stops. Each player has five shoves in a round.
Round 1 is on the bare table. Round 2 is on the table dusted with a pinch of talcum powder. Round 3 is on a bedsheet pulled flat.
Add up each round. The player with the most points after three rounds wins.
Playing alone: try to beat your own score for each round on a second go.

setup.art: A smooth table with a start line at the near edge and a target line 60 centimetres away, and a ruler lying between them.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a start line and a target line 60 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A child's finger shoving a coin from behind the start line.
setup.caption: 2. Shove the coin once and let go.

setup.art: A hand sprinkling a pinch of talcum powder on the table between the two lines.
setup.caption: 3. For round 2, dust the table with powder. For round 3, lay a bedsheet.

flow.do: 1. Choose a smooth table at least 1 metre long. 2. Mark the start line and the target line 60 centimetres apart. 3. Give each player a coin of the same kind. 4. Let each player try three practice shoves.
flow.say: The aim is to stop the coin on the far line. Your finger gives the coin its speed. After that, only friction acts along the table.
flow.kid: Mark two lines 60 cm apart. Take a coin. Try three practice shoves.
flow.parent: A dining table, a carrom board or a smooth floor all work. A coin can scratch polished wood, so put the lines on a surface that will not be spoiled.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shove Coin. Here you mark the lines and practise.

flow.do: 1. Play round 1 on the bare table, five shoves each. 2. Write down the points. 3. Ask how hard the shove had to be.
flow.say: Round 1 is on the bare table. How hard a shove gets the coin to the line and no further?
flow.kid: Play round 1. Shove the coin five times. Write your points.

ask.q: What stops the coin after your finger lets go?
good: Friction between the coin and the table.
Sliding friction turns the coin's movement into heat.

flow.context: This is round 1 of Shove Coin. Here you shove the coin along the bare table.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a pinch of talcum powder between the lines and spread it with a dry hand. 2. Ask for a guess: harder or gentler shoves now? 3. Play round 2. 4. Wipe the table, lay a bedsheet flat over it and play round 3.
flow.say: The powder changes the friction. Will you need a harder shove or a gentler one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Dust the table with powder. Guess first: harder shove or gentler? Play round 2. Then play round 3 on a bedsheet.
flow.parent: With powder the coin slides much further, so most players overshoot at first. On the bedsheet a much harder shove is needed. Wipe the powder up with a damp cloth afterwards, because a powdered floor is slippery.
flow.context: This is rounds 2 and 3 of Shove Coin. Here you change the friction with powder and then with a bedsheet.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points for each round. 2. Fill in the last two lines of the score sheet. 3. Talk about what changed.
flow.say: On which surface did the coin need the hardest shove? What does that tell us about the friction there?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which surface needed the hardest shove? Why?

check.q: On a table dusted with powder, the same shove sends a coin further. Why?
options: The powder gives the coin extra speed
The powder makes friction smaller, so the coin's energy lasts longer
The powder makes the coin lighter
check.why: The shove gives the coin the same kinetic energy as before. Powder is a lubricant, so the friction force is smaller and the energy lasts for a longer slide. The powder does not push the coin or change its weight.

flow.context: This is the last step of Shove Coin. Here you add up the points and compare the three surfaces.

experiments.title: The Stopping Distance Test: how far does a marble roll before it stops?
experiments.context: In this experiment a marble rolls down a cardboard channel onto a cloth on the floor. You measure how far the marble rolls before it stops. First you change the cloth, and then you change how high the marble starts.
experiments.question: How does the surface change the distance a rolling marble needs to stop? And if the marble starts twice as high up the ramp, how much further does it roll?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On which will the marble stop sooner, a bath towel or a cotton bedsheet? Then guess again. If the marble starts twice as far up the ramp, how far will it roll? Choose the same distance, twice as far, or more than twice as far. Write both guesses and your reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: In part 1, change only the surface. Start the marble at the 20 centimetre mark every time. In part 2, change only the start mark, and keep the towel. Always let go of the marble without a push. Use the same marble, the same ramp and the same pile of books. Do every run 3 times and find the mean, because one run can be a fluke.

materials.item: a glass marble (a small rubber ball or a toy car also works)
a strip of stiff cardboard about 40 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide, cut from a carton
books to make a pile 6 centimetres high
a bath towel
a cotton bedsheet
one more surface of your choice, such as a folded blanket, a doormat, a yoga mat or newspaper
a measuring tape or a 30 centimetre ruler
sticky tape, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Pick up the marble after every run, so that nobody steps on it. Keep marbles away from children under three.

schedule.what: Build the ramp. Roll the marble on three surfaces, then from three start marks. Find the means and draw two charts.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with every run and every mean. Draw a bar chart of the three surfaces, and a line graph of the three start marks. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean stopping distance from the 20 centimetre mark
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A strip of cardboard folded into a V-shaped channel, with its top end resting on a pile of three books and its bottom end resting on a bath towel spread on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the cardboard into a channel. Rest the top on books 6 centimetres high and the bottom on the towel.

setup.art: The cardboard channel seen from the side with three pencil marks labelled 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from the bottom end, and a finger holding a marble on the 20 mark.
setup.caption: 2. Mark 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from the bottom end. Hold the marble on a mark and let go.

setup.art: A marble at rest on a towel and a measuring tape stretched from the bottom end of the channel to the marble.
setup.caption: 3. Measure from the end of the channel to the place where the marble stops.

flow.do: 1. Fold the cardboard strip along its length to make a V-shaped channel. 2. Rest one end on a pile of books 6 centimetres high, and tape it there. 3. Spread the towel flat on the floor and rest the bottom end of the channel on it. 4. Mark the channel 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from the bottom end.
flow.say: We are going to roll a marble down this channel and see how far it goes. First let's build the ramp and mark three starting places.
flow.kid: Fold the cardboard into a V. Rest the top on the books. Rest the bottom on the towel. Mark 10, 20 and 30 cm from the bottom.
flow.parent: Measure the marks along the channel from its bottom end. The bottom end must lie on the cloth, so the marble meets no step. A toy car needs no channel: use a tray or a hardback book as the ramp.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stopping Distance Test. Here you build a ramp with three start marks.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the towel and the bedsheet. 2. Ask for the first guess and its reason. 3. Ask for the second guess, about starting twice as high, and its reason. 4. Write both down.
flow.say: On which cloth will the marble stop sooner? And if it starts twice as far up, how much further will it roll? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which cloth stops the marble sooner. Guess what starting twice as high does. Say why. Write it down.

good: The towel is soft and rough, so it has more friction.
A higher start makes the marble faster, so it needs longer to stop.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the higher start to make only a small difference.
flow.context: This step of the Stopping Distance Test is for guessing. You guess before you roll the marble.

flow.do: 1. Hold the marble on the 30 centimetre mark with one finger. 2. Lift the finger straight up. 3. Watch where the marble stops. 4. If it rolls off the end of the towel, take one book away and try again.
flow.say: This is a trial run from the top mark. We need the marble to stop on the towel. Lift your finger straight up, and do not push.
flow.kid: Hold the marble on the top mark. Lift your finger. Do not push. Does it stop on the towel?
flow.parent: If the marble stops within 10 centimetres, add a book. Once the ramp is right, do not change it again. Then roll the marble once onto the bare floor, to see how far it goes with little friction.
flow.context: This step of the Stopping Distance Test is a trial run. It checks that the marble stops on the towel.

flow.do: 1. Start the marble at the 20 centimetre mark. 2. Measure from the end of the channel to the marble. 3. Do 3 runs on the towel and write each one down. 4. Lay the bedsheet flat in place of the towel and do 3 runs. 5. Do 3 runs on your third surface.
flow.say: Part 1 changes only the surface. Start at the 20 centimetre mark every time. Measure in a straight line from the end of the channel.
flow.kid: Start at the 20 cm mark each time. Do 3 runs on the towel. Do 3 on the bedsheet. Do 3 on your own surface.
flow.parent: Pull the bedsheet smooth and hold its corners down with books. If the marble rolls off the end of the sheet, write 'more than' and the length of the sheet.
flow.context: This is part 1 of the Stopping Distance Test. Here you roll the marble from the same mark onto three surfaces.

flow.do: 1. Put the towel back. 2. Ask your child to guess the distances from the 10 and the 30 centimetre marks. They can use the result from the 20 centimetre mark. 3. Do 3 runs from the 10 centimetre mark. 4. Do 3 runs from the 30 centimetre mark.
flow.say: Part 2 changes only the start mark. From the 20 centimetre mark you already have a mean. What do you expect from 10 and from 30? Why?
flow.kid: Put the towel back. Guess the distance from the 10 cm mark. Guess for the 30 cm mark. Do 3 runs from each.

ask.q: What do you expect from the 10 centimetre mark, and why?
good: About half as far, because the marble starts half as high.
Less, because the marble is slower at the bottom.

flow.context: This is part 2 of the Stopping Distance Test. Here you roll the marble onto the towel from three start marks.

flow.do: 1. For each row, add the three runs and divide by 3. 2. Draw a bar chart of the three surfaces. 3. Draw a line graph of stopping distance against start mark for the towel.
flow.say: Let's find the mean for each row. Then we draw one bar for each surface, and one point for each start mark.
flow.kid: Add the three runs. Divide by 3. Draw a bar for each surface. Draw a point for each start mark.
flow.parent: If one run is very different from the other two, ask what happened. Roll it again and say so in the table. A mean hides a mistake, so look at the three runs first.
flow.context: This step of the Stopping Distance Test is for the means and the two charts.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask them to draw the marble on the towel with a friction arrow. 3. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then draw the marble on the towel. Which way does the friction arrow point?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Draw the marble and a friction arrow.

ask.q: The marble had the same speed at the bottom each time in part 1. Why did it stop sooner on the towel?
good: The towel pushes against the marble with a bigger force.
The towel takes the marble's energy away in a shorter distance.

ask.q: In part 2, where did the extra distance come from?
good: A higher start gives the marble more energy.
The towel takes away about the same energy each centimetre, so more energy lasts longer.

flow.parent: Expect about double the distance from double the start mark, not exactly double. Real cloth gives results between about one and a half and two and a half times.

check.q: In the Stopping Distance Test, the marble started twice as far up the ramp and rolled about twice as far. Why?
options: The marble was heavier the second time
The marble had about twice the energy to lose
The towel became smoother
check.why: Starting twice as high gives the marble about twice the kinetic energy at the bottom. The towel takes away about the same energy in every centimetre, so twice the energy lasts about twice the distance. The marble and the towel did not change.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Stopping Distance Test. Here you explain your results and draw the friction arrow.

experiments.title: The Warm Coin Test: what makes friction make more heat?
experiments.context: In this experiment one person rubs a coin on cardboard. A second person, with eyes closed, judges how warm the coin is. You change the number of strokes, and then how hard you press.
experiments.question: Does a coin get warmer if you rub it for more strokes? Does it get warmer if you press harder? And can a judge tell without being told what was done?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will be warmest: a coin rubbed for 20 strokes, 40 strokes or 80 strokes? Will a firm press or a light press make the coin warmer? Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Use coins of the same kind, and start each test with a cool coin. Rub between the same two lines, 20 centimetres apart, at the same speed. In the first test change only the number of strokes. In the second test change only the press. The judge keeps their eyes closed and is not told what was done. Then the judge's guess cannot change the score.

materials.item: coins of the same kind, such as 5 rupee coins
a piece of thick cardboard at least 25 centimetres long, such as the back of an old notebook
a ruler and a pencil
a steel plate, to cool the coins on between tests
a notebook for the table of results

experiments.safety: A coin rubbed hard for 80 strokes can be hot enough to sting. Touch it to the skin for one second only. Never press a hot coin on anybody as a joke.

schedule.what: Rub a coin for 20, 40 and 80 strokes, then with a light and a firm press. A judge with closed eyes scores the warmth each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

setup.art: A piece of thick cardboard on a table with two pencil lines drawn 20 centimetres apart, and three coins on a steel plate beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two lines 20 centimetres apart on the cardboard. Keep the coins on a steel plate.

setup.art: A child's fingertips pressing a coin flat on the cardboard and rubbing it fast between the two lines.
setup.caption: 2. Press the coin flat and rub it from line to line. Each trip is one stroke.

setup.art: A grown-up with closed eyes holding out an arm, and a child touching the coin to the inside of the grown-up's wrist.
setup.caption: 3. Touch the coin to the judge's wrist for one second. The judge gives a score from 0 to 3.

flow.do: 1. Draw two lines 20 centimetres apart on the cardboard. 2. Put the three coins on the steel plate. 3. Agree the scores: 0 is cool, 1 is the same as skin, 2 is warm, 3 is hot. 4. Practise 10 strokes at about 4 strokes each second.
flow.say: We will rub a coin and feel how warm it gets. One trip from line to line is one stroke. Let's agree what the scores 0, 1, 2 and 3 mean.
flow.kid: Draw two lines 20 cm apart. Put the coins on the plate. Learn the scores 0 to 3. Practise 10 fast strokes.
flow.parent: Hold the coin flat under two fingertips. The cardboard protects the table and holds the heat in the coin.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Warm Coin Test. Here you set up the cardboard, the coins and the scores.

flow.do: 1. Ask which number of strokes will make the warmest coin, and why. 2. Ask whether a firm or a light press will make more heat, and why. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Which coin will be warmest: 20 strokes, 40 strokes or 80 strokes? Will pressing harder change the warmth? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which coin will be warmest. Guess what a firm press does. Say why. Write it down.

good: More strokes means more rubbing, so more heat.
Pressing harder makes more friction, so more heat.

flow.context: This step of the Warm Coin Test is for guessing. You guess before you rub the coin.

flow.do: 1. The judge closes their eyes and holds out a wrist. 2. The rubber picks 20, 40 or 80 strokes in secret and rubs with a firm press. 3. The rubber touches the coin to the judge's wrist for one second. 4. The judge gives a score. 5. Repeat with a cool coin until all three numbers are done.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will not tell you how many strokes I did. Tell me the score when you feel the coin.
flow.kid: The judge closes their eyes. Rub the coin 20, 40 or 80 strokes. Touch the judge's wrist for one second. Write the score.
flow.parent: Take turns as rubber and judge. Put each used coin back on the steel plate for two minutes, because the plate cools it. If nothing feels warm, rub faster and press harder, or double every number of strokes.
flow.context: This is the strokes test of the Warm Coin Test. Here a judge with closed eyes scores coins rubbed for 20, 40 and 80 strokes.

flow.do: 1. Take a cool coin. 2. Rub it for 40 strokes with a light press, as if you might tear the cardboard. 3. The judge scores it. 4. Rub a cool coin for 40 strokes with a firm press. 5. The judge scores it. Do the two in a secret order.
flow.say: Now the strokes stay the same and only the press changes. I will do the light press and the firm press in a secret order.
flow.kid: Rub 40 strokes with a light press. Then rub 40 strokes with a firm press. The judge scores each one.
flow.context: This is the press test of the Warm Coin Test. Here the number of strokes stays at 40 and only the press changes.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to choose one more change. 2. Ask what they expect, and why. 3. Test it with 40 firm strokes and a judge with closed eyes.
flow.say: Now you design a test. You could try a drop of oil on the cardboard, a smooth steel plate, or longer strokes. What do you expect, and why?
flow.kid: Choose one more change. Guess what it will do. Say why. Test it with 40 strokes.
flow.parent: Oil makes the friction smaller, so the coin usually stays cooler. The difference can be small. If the judge feels no difference, write that down as the result.
flow.context: This step of the Warm Coin Test lets you choose and test one more change.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child for the three sentences. 3. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Where did the heat in the coin come from?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Where did the heat in the coin come from?
good: From the movement of my hand.
Friction turned the kinetic energy of the rubbing into heat.

ask.q: Why did the judge keep their eyes closed?
good: So the judge could not guess the answer from what they saw.
If you expect a coin to be hot, it can feel hotter.

check.q: In the Warm Coin Test, a firm press warmed the coin more than a light press. Why?
options: A firm press makes a bigger friction force
A firm press squeezes heat out of the fingers
A firm press makes the coin slide faster
check.why: Pressing harder makes the friction force bigger. The energy turned into heat is the friction force multiplied by the distance rubbed. So the same strokes with a bigger force make more heat. The speed and the strokes stayed the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Warm Coin Test. Here you explain what made the coin warmer.

activities.title: Finger Walk: which way does friction push?
activities.context: In this activity two fingers walk across a loose sheet of paper. Then a foot pushes on a loose sheet of newspaper. You watch which way the paper moves, to find out which way friction pushes a walker.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper
a smooth table top, a steel tray or a large steel plate
a sheet of newspaper and a chair on a smooth floor
sticky tape, a pencil and a notebook

activities.safety: Do the foot test sitting on a chair. Do not stand or run on loose paper, because it slips.
activities.record: Draw the walking fingers and the paper. Add one arrow for the push of the fingers on the paper, and one for the friction on the fingers.

setup.art: Two fingers of a child's hand walking like legs across a loose sheet of paper on a smooth table, with the paper sliding backward.
setup.caption: 1. Walk two fingers forward across a loose sheet of paper.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with one foot on a sheet of newspaper on a tiled floor, pushing the paper backward.
setup.caption: 2. Sit down, put one foot on newspaper and push as if to walk.

setup.art: The same sheet of paper taped to the table at its corners, with the two fingers walking forward across it.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the paper down and walk the fingers again.

flow.do: 1. Lay the sheet of paper on the smooth table. 2. Ask your child which way the paper will move when two fingers walk forward on it, and why. 3. Your child presses two fingertips on the paper and walks them forward like legs.
flow.say: Your fingers are going to walk forward on this loose paper. Which way will the paper move? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which way the paper will move. Say why. Now walk two fingers forward on the paper.
flow.parent: The paper slides backward, and the fingers hardly move forward. Press down a little, as a foot does.
flow.context: This is the first step of Finger Walk. Here two fingers walk across a loose sheet of paper.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on a chair on a smooth floor. 2. Put a sheet of newspaper under one foot. 3. Your child pushes with that foot as if starting to walk forward.
flow.say: Stay sitting. Push with your foot as if you were starting to walk. Which way does your foot push the paper?
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. Put one foot on the newspaper. Push as if to walk. Watch the paper.

ask.q: Which way does your foot push on the floor when you walk forward?
good: Backward.
My foot pushes the floor back, and the paper showed it.

flow.context: This step of Finger Walk repeats the test with a foot on a loose sheet of newspaper.

flow.do: 1. Tape the corners of the plain paper to the table. 2. Your child walks two fingers forward again. 3. Ask what pushes the fingers forward now. 4. Your child draws the fingers with two arrows.
flow.say: Now the paper cannot slide. Your fingers push it backward as before. So what pushes your fingers forward?
flow.kid: Tape the paper down. Walk your fingers again. What pushes them forward now? Draw two arrows.
flow.parent: One arrow shows the fingers pushing the paper backward. The other shows friction from the paper pushing the fingers forward. The two arrows are the same length.

check.q: In Finger Walk, the loose paper slid backward when the fingers walked forward. What does that show?
options: The paper was too light
The fingers push backward on the paper
Friction pushes the fingers backward
check.why: The paper moved the way it was pushed, which was backward. So walking fingers push backward on what is under them. Friction from the paper pushes the fingers forward. Choosing 'friction pushes the fingers backward' usually means using the rule 'friction is against the movement'.

flow.context: This is the last step of Finger Walk. Here the paper is taped down, and you draw the forces.

activities.title: The Riding Katori: can friction start a thing moving?
activities.context: In this activity a katori, a small steel bowl, stands on a cloth. You pull the cloth slowly, stop it suddenly, and then pull it very fast. Each time you work out which way friction pushed the katori.

materials.item: an empty steel katori (a small steel bowl)
a cotton napkin, a hand towel or a sheet of newspaper
a smooth table
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the katori three times: for the slow pull, the sudden stop and the fast pull. Add a friction arrow to each drawing.

setup.art: An empty steel katori standing on a cotton napkin spread on a table, with a child's hands holding the near edge of the napkin.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the katori on the cloth. Pull the cloth slowly.

setup.art: The napkin stopped and the katori sliding a little way forward across it.
setup.caption: 2. Pull steadily, then stop the cloth suddenly.

setup.art: The napkin whipped out fast from under the katori, which stays almost where it was on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the cloth out very fast.

flow.do: 1. Spread the cloth on the table and stand the katori on it. 2. Ask what the katori will do when the cloth is pulled slowly, and why. 3. Your child pulls the cloth slowly and steadily towards themself.
flow.say: I will not touch the katori. What will it do when you pull the cloth slowly? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the katori will do. Say why. Pull the cloth slowly towards you.

ask.q: Only the cloth touched the katori. So which force made the katori move?
good: Friction from the cloth.
Friction pushed the katori the same way the cloth moved.

flow.parent: The katori rides along with the cloth. Let your child say which force moved it before you say so.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Riding Katori. Here you pull a cloth slowly from under a steel bowl.

flow.do: 1. Your child pulls the cloth steadily, then stops it suddenly. 2. Watch the katori. 3. Ask which way friction pushed the katori this time.
flow.say: Pull steadily, then stop the cloth all at once. Watch the katori. Which way did friction push it just now?
flow.kid: Pull steadily. Stop the cloth suddenly. Watch the katori. Which way did friction push it?
flow.parent: The katori slides forward a little over the stopped cloth and then stops. Now friction pushes it backward. In both steps, friction worked to make the katori and the cloth move together.
flow.context: This step of the Riding Katori stops the cloth suddenly, to see what friction does to the moving bowl.

flow.do: 1. Put the katori near the far edge of the cloth. 2. Your child grips the near edge with both hands and pulls it out very fast, straight and level. 3. Compare with the slow pull.
flow.say: Now pull the cloth out as fast as you can. Guess first. Will the katori ride along this time?
flow.kid: Guess first. Pull the cloth out very fast. Did the katori ride along?
flow.parent: The katori stays almost where it was. Friction has a limit, and it cannot speed the katori up that quickly. Use an empty katori, so nothing spills.
flow.context: This step of the Riding Katori pulls the cloth out very fast, to find the limit of friction.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the katori for all three pulls. 2. They add a friction arrow to each drawing. 3. Ask what is the same about all three.
flow.say: Draw the three pulls and the friction arrow for each. Friction pointed a different way each time. What was it doing every time?
flow.kid: Draw the three pulls. Add a friction arrow to each. What did friction do every time?

check.q: A katori stands on a cloth. The cloth is pulled slowly and the katori moves with it. Which force moved the katori?
options: Gravity
Friction from the cloth
The push of the air
check.why: Only the cloth touched the katori, and friction is the force between touching surfaces. Friction from the cloth pushed the katori the way the cloth moved. Gravity pulls down, not sideways, and the air hardly pushes at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Riding Katori. Here you draw the friction arrows and find the rule.

activities.title: Green and Red: a friction map of one machine
activities.context: In this activity you draw one machine, such as a bicycle. You mark where friction is wanted in green, and where it is unwanted in red.

materials.item: a bicycle. If you have none, use a door with its hinges, handle and bolt, and a pair of chappals
a green and a red sketch pen or crayon
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Keep fingers away from the chain and the spokes while a wheel is turning.
activities.record: Keep the drawing with its green and red marks. Under it write one sentence for each mark, saying what the friction does there.

setup.art: A child's pencil drawing of a bicycle seen from the side, lying next to a real bicycle on its stand.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the machine from the side.

setup.art: The same drawing with green marks on the tyres, brake pads, pedals and handle grips, and red marks on the axles and the chain.
setup.caption: 2. Mark green where friction is wanted and red where it is unwanted.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bicycle safely. 2. Your child draws it from the side, big enough to fill the page. 3. Together, name the parts: tyres, brake pads, rim, pedals, chain, axles, handle grips and seat.
flow.say: Let's draw the cycle and name its parts. Then we will hunt for every place where two surfaces touch.
flow.kid: Draw the cycle from the side. Fill the page. Name each part.
flow.context: This is the first step of Green and Red. Here you draw one machine and name its parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child touches each place where two surfaces meet. 2. For each place ask: do we want these to slide, or to grip? 3. Mark green for grip wanted and red for sliding wanted. 4. Find at least four green places and three red ones.
flow.say: Touch each place where two surfaces meet. Do we want them to grip here, or to slide easily? Why?
flow.kid: Touch each place where two surfaces meet. Grip wanted is green. Sliding wanted is red. Find seven places.

ask.q: The brake pad and the axle are a hand's width apart. Why does one need friction and the other need oil?
good: The pad must grip the rim to stop the wheel.
The axle must turn easily, or the rider's effort is wasted as heat.

flow.parent: Green: tyres on the road, brake pads on the rim, shoes on the pedals, hands on the grips, the seat. Red: the axles, the chain links, the pedal axle and the brake cable in its tube. On a door, the hinge and bolt are red and the handle is green.
flow.context: This step of Green and Red marks each touching place on the machine green or red.

flow.do: 1. Pick one green place and one red place. 2. Ask what would go wrong if the friction there were the other way round. 3. Ask how people made the friction bigger or smaller at each place.
flow.say: Choose one green place and one red place. What would go wrong if we swapped them? How did the makers get the friction they wanted?
flow.kid: Pick one green place and one red place. What if they were swapped? How did the makers change the friction?

check.q: Which part of a bicycle is oiled to make friction smaller?
options: The brake pads
The tyres
The chain
check.why: The links of the chain must slide over each other easily, so the chain is oiled. Oil on brake pads or tyres would be dangerous, because those parts must grip.

flow.context: This is the last step of Green and Red. Here you say what each friction is for and how it was made.

activities.title: Hand in the Bucket: water resistance and upthrust
activities.context: In this activity you sweep your hand through a bucket of water in different ways. Then you push an empty bottle under the water. You feel two forces from water: water resistance and upthrust.

materials.item: a bucket at least half full of water, in the bathroom or on a balcony
an empty plastic bottle of about 500 millilitres, with its cap screwed on
a steel plate
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Wipe up any water on the floor at once, because a wet floor has little friction. Use the water for mopping or for plants afterwards.
activities.record: Write which sweep was hardest and which was easiest. Draw the bottle under water with an arrow for upthrust.

setup.art: A child's hand held flat like a paddle, sweeping through the water in a bucket.
setup.caption: 1. Sweep a flat hand through the water. Then sweep it edge-on.

setup.art: A hand pushing a closed empty plastic bottle down into a bucket of water.
setup.caption: 2. Push the empty bottle under the water and hold it still.

flow.do: 1. Ask which will be harder to sweep through water, a flat hand or a hand held edge-on, and why. 2. Your child sweeps a flat hand across the bucket. 3. They sweep the hand edge-on at the same speed.
flow.say: Which will be harder to move through the water, a flat hand or the edge of your hand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which is harder, flat hand or edge-on. Say why. Now sweep your hand both ways.
flow.parent: The flat hand pushes a much bigger front through the water, so the water resistance is much bigger.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hand in the Bucket. Here you compare a flat hand with a hand held edge-on.

flow.do: 1. Your child sweeps the flat hand very slowly. 2. Then they sweep it fast. 3. Ask how the push of the water changed.
flow.say: Now keep your hand flat. Sweep it slowly, then fast. How does the push of the water change?
flow.kid: Keep your hand flat. Sweep slowly. Then sweep fast. What changed?

ask.q: When your hand is still in the water, how much water resistance do you feel?
good: None.
Water resistance acts only when my hand moves through the water.

flow.context: This step of Hand in the Bucket changes the speed of the hand, to see how water resistance changes.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the closed empty bottle down into the water. 2. They hold it still under the water. 3. They let go and watch.
flow.say: Push the bottle under and hold it still. Do you feel a force now, though nothing is moving? Which way does it push?
flow.kid: Push the bottle under the water. Hold it still. Which way does the water push it? Let go.
flow.parent: The water pushes the bottle up even when the bottle is still. That is upthrust. Water resistance acts only on a moving thing, and it points against the movement.
flow.context: This step of Hand in the Bucket pushes an empty bottle under water, to feel upthrust.

flow.do: 1. Your child waves the steel plate flat-on through the air, then edge-on. 2. Ask what the air did. 3. They write down how water resistance, air resistance and upthrust differ.
flow.say: Wave the plate flat-on, then edge-on. Air does the same as water, only more weakly. Now tell me how upthrust is different from water resistance.
flow.kid: Wave the plate flat-on. Wave it edge-on. What did the air do? How is upthrust different?

check.q: You hold an empty bottle still under water. Which force from the water pushes on the bottle?
options: Water resistance, pushing backward
Upthrust, pushing up
No force, because nothing moves
check.why: Upthrust is the upward push of water on a thing that is in it. It acts even when the thing is still. Water resistance acts only when a thing moves through the water.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hand in the Bucket. Here you feel air resistance and compare the three forces.

activities.title: Friction Arrows: draw the forces on five things
activities.context: In this activity you set up five small scenes with a book, a board and a katori. For each one you draw a force diagram with a friction arrow.

materials.item: a hardback book
a tray, a chopping board or a second large book, to make a slope
a katori and a cloth, and a sheet of paper for walking fingers
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Draw five force diagrams, one for each scene. Label the friction arrow in each. Under the last one, write the rule for the direction of friction.

setup.art: A hardback book sliding across a table after a push, with a pencil arrow drawn in a notebook beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Set up each scene and watch what slides, or would slide.

setup.art: A notebook page with five small force diagrams: a sliding book, a book on a slope, a book against a wall, walking fingers and a katori on a cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each thing as a box with a labelled friction arrow.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the book across the table and lets go. 2. They draw the book as a box, with an arrow showing which way it moves. 3. They add the friction arrow and label it.
flow.say: Push the book and let go. It slows down. Draw the book, and draw the friction arrow. Which way does it point, and why?
flow.kid: Push the book and let go. Draw it as a box. Add the friction arrow. Say why.
flow.parent: The friction arrow lies along the table and points against the slide. It starts where the book touches the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Friction Arrows. Here you draw the friction on a book sliding across a table.

flow.do: 1. Rest the book on the tray. 2. Lift one end of the tray a little, so the book stays put. 3. Ask which way the book would slide with no friction. 4. Your child draws the book and the friction arrow.
flow.say: The book is not moving. Is there friction on it? Which way would the book slide if the tray were perfectly slippery?
flow.kid: Rest the book on the tilted tray. Which way would it slide? Draw the friction arrow.

ask.q: The book is still. How do you know friction is acting on it?
good: Without friction the book would slide down the slope.
Something must balance the pull down the slope.

flow.context: This step of Friction Arrows draws the friction on a book resting on a slope.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses the book flat against a wall with one hand. 2. They ease the press until the book starts to slip, then press again. 3. They draw the book and the friction arrow.
flow.say: Hold the book against the wall with a flat hand. Gravity pulls it down. What holds it up? Which way does that force point?
flow.kid: Press the book on the wall. Ease off until it slips. Press again. Draw the friction arrow.
flow.parent: Friction from the wall and from the hand points up. A lighter press gives less friction, so the book slips.
flow.context: This step of Friction Arrows draws the friction on a book pressed against a wall.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks two fingers on a taped sheet of paper and draws the friction on the fingers. 2. They pull a cloth slowly with the katori on it and draw the friction on the katori.
flow.say: Now draw two things that friction pushes forward: your walking fingers and the katori on the moving cloth.
flow.kid: Walk your fingers on taped paper. Pull the cloth with the katori on it. Draw both friction arrows.
flow.context: This step of Friction Arrows draws two cases where friction points the way the thing moves.

flow.do: 1. Lay the five drawings side by side. 2. Ask what one rule gives the direction of friction in all five. 3. Your child writes the rule in their own words.
flow.say: Look at all five arrows. They point backward, up a slope, straight up and forward. What one rule fits them all?
flow.kid: Look at your five arrows. What one rule fits them all? Write it down.
flow.parent: A good rule: friction on a thing points against the way that thing slides, or would slide, over the surface it touches.

check.q: A book rests on a tilted tray and does not slide. Which way does friction push the book?
options: Down the slope
Up the slope
There is no friction on a still book
check.why: Without friction the book would slide down the slope. Friction acts against that slide, so it points up the slope. A thing that is still can have friction on it. That friction is called static friction.

flow.context: This is the last step of Friction Arrows. Here you find one rule for the direction of friction.

activities.title: Pencil, Eraser, Match: three frictions we use on purpose
activities.context: In this activity you write with a pencil, rub the mark out and watch a grown-up strike a match. Each one uses friction on purpose: two use wear, and one uses heat.

materials.item: a soft, dark pencil and an eraser
a sheet of white paper
a box of safety matches and a steel plate, for the grown-up

activities.safety: Only a grown-up strikes the match. Strike it away from the body, hold it over the steel plate, and dip the used match in water.
activities.record: Write one sentence for each of the three: what rubbed against what, and what the friction did.

setup.art: A child shading a dark patch on white paper with a pencil, with a grey smudge on one fingertip.
setup.caption: 1. Shade a dark patch with the pencil. Rub it with a finger.

setup.art: An eraser rubbing out half of the dark patch, with a small heap of grey crumbs beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Rub out half the patch and collect the crumbs.

setup.art: A grown-up striking a match on the side of a matchbox, held over a steel plate.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up strikes one match.

flow.do: 1. Your child shades a patch about as big as a matchbox, pressing firmly. 2. They rub the patch with a clean fingertip and look at the finger. 3. Ask where the grey came from.
flow.say: Shade a dark patch and rub it with your finger. Where did the grey on your finger come from? How did it get onto the paper?
flow.kid: Shade a dark patch. Rub it with a clean finger. Where did the grey come from?
flow.parent: The pencil tip is graphite mixed with clay. Friction with the rough paper pulls thin flakes of graphite off the tip. Writing is wear that we want.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pencil, Eraser, Match. Here you find out how a pencil leaves a mark.

flow.do: 1. Your child rubs out half the patch with the eraser. 2. They sweep the crumbs into a small heap and look at their colour. 3. Ask where the pencil mark has gone.
flow.say: Rub out half the patch and collect the crumbs. Look at their colour. Where has the pencil mark gone?
flow.kid: Rub out half the patch. Collect the crumbs. Look at their colour. Where did the mark go?

ask.q: Why does an eraser get smaller as you use it?
good: Friction wears bits of rubber off.
The crumbs carry the graphite away, so the eraser must wear to work.

flow.context: This step of Pencil, Eraser, Match finds out how an eraser removes a pencil mark.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up strikes one match on the side of the box, over the steel plate. 2. Watch the moment it lights. 3. The grown-up dips the used match in water.
flow.say: Watch the match head as I drag it along the box. What does the rubbing do just before the flame starts?
flow.kid: Watch a grown-up strike a match. What does the rubbing do before the flame starts?
flow.parent: The strip on the box holds red phosphorus and fine ground glass. Dragging the match head along it makes heat by friction. The heat starts the chemicals in the match head burning.
flow.context: This step of Pencil, Eraser, Match watches friction light a match.

flow.do: 1. Ask which of the three used wear and which used heat. 2. Your child writes one sentence for each.
flow.say: We used friction three times on purpose. Which times did we use wear? Which time did we use heat?
flow.kid: Which ones used wear? Which one used heat? Write a sentence for each.

check.q: How does a pencil leave a mark on paper?
options: Friction pulls thin flakes of graphite off the tip
The pencil melts onto the paper
Ink flows out of the tip
check.why: The paper is rough, and friction with it pulls thin flakes of graphite off the pencil tip. The flakes stay on the paper as the mark. Nothing melts, and a pencil holds no ink.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pencil, Eraser, Match. Here you sort the three uses of friction.

projects.title: The Home Friction Service: fix five frictions in three days
projects.context: In this three-day project you find three places at home with too much friction and two places with too little. You fix each one with something from the house, and test it again.

materials.item: cooking oil or machine oil, and a cotton bud
a candle stub or a dry bar of soap
rubber bands
a cotton cloth that can be made damp
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: A grown-up puts oil on hinges and on anything high up. Wipe spilt oil off the floor at once. Never put oil, wax or soap on a floor, a stair, a cycle's rim or a tyre.

schedule.what: Walk round the home. Find three places with too much friction and two with too little. Give each one a trouble score from 0 to 3.
Fix each place with oil, wax, soap, rubber bands or a damp cloth.
Test each place again, give it a new score and write a service card.

projects.record: Make a table with five rows: the place, the trouble, the score before, what you did, and the score after. On the last day write which fix worked best and why.

setup.art: A child with a notebook listening to a squeaking door hinge, with a stuck drawer and a sliding chopping board in the background.
setup.caption: 1. Find three places with too much friction and two with too little.

setup.art: A grown-up putting a drop of oil on a door hinge with a cotton bud while a child rubs a candle stub along a zip.
setup.caption: 2. Fix each one: oil, wax or soap for less friction, rubber or a damp cloth for more.

setup.art: A notebook table with five rows, showing a score before and a score after for each place.
setup.caption: 3. Test again and write the new scores.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together. 2. Find three things that stick or squeak, such as a hinge, a drawer, a zip or a window bolt. 3. Find two things that slip, such as a chopping board, a jar lid, a rug or clothes on a hanger. 4. Score each one from 0 for no trouble to 3 for a lot.
flow.say: Let's be friction engineers for our home. Where is there too much friction? Where is there too little? Give each place a score.
flow.kid: Find three things that stick or squeak. Find two things that slip. Give each a score from 0 to 3.
flow.parent: Let your child choose the places. A good list has both kinds: friction to make smaller and friction to make bigger.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Home Friction Service. Here you find five friction troubles and score them.

flow.do: 1. For a hinge or a bolt, a grown-up adds one drop of oil with a cotton bud. 2. For a drawer or a zip, rub the candle or dry soap along the sliding parts. 3. For a jar lid or a hanger, wind a rubber band round it. 4. For a chopping board or a rug, put a damp cloth or a rubber mat underneath.
flow.say: For each place, ask one question. Do we want less friction here, or more? Then choose the fix and say why it should work.
flow.kid: For each place, ask: less friction or more? Choose a fix. Say why it should work. Then do it.

ask.q: Why does wax help a zip but a rubber band help a jar lid?
good: Wax is a lubricant, so it makes friction smaller.
Rubber grips well, so it makes friction bigger.

flow.parent: Wax and soap work well on zips and wooden drawers. Oil suits metal hinges and bolts. Wipe away extra oil, because oil collects dust.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Home Friction Service. Here you fix each friction trouble.

flow.do: 1. Test each of the five places again. 2. Give each a new score. 3. Your child writes a service card: what was done, and when to check again.
flow.say: Did each fix work? Which one worked best? Which one may wear off, and why?
flow.kid: Test all five again. Give new scores. Which fix worked best? Write your service card.

check.q: A chopping board slides on the kitchen counter while you cut. Which fix makes sense?
options: A drop of oil under the board
A damp cloth under the board
Polishing the counter
check.why: The board needs more friction, and a damp cloth grips both the board and the counter. Oil and polish are for making friction smaller, so the board would slide more.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Home Friction Service. Here you test the five places again and write up the results.

challenges.title: The Escape Lane: stop a runaway marble in 20 centimetres
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Stopping Distance Test, a marble rolled off a ramp and a long way across a bedsheet. Here you design a surface that stops the same marble in a very short distance.
challenges.problem: Let a marble go from the 30 centimetre mark of the Stopping Distance ramp. It must stop within 20 centimetres of the end of the channel. Only the surface under the marble may stop it.
constraints: Nothing may stand in the marble's way: no walls, bumps or holes.
The marble must start from the 30 centimetre mark, with no push.
Use only things from home, and leave the ramp as it was in the Stopping Distance Test.
materials: the ramp and the marble from the Stopping Distance Test
a large tray or steel plate
about two cups of uncooked rice or dal, washed afterwards for cooking
general: Fold a towel in four, so the marble rolls on a thick, soft surface.
Lay a folded blanket at the end of the ramp.
creative: Fill a large tray with uncooked rice one centimetre deep, and rest the end of the channel inside it. Beds of loose gravel stop runaway lorries on some steep roads in the same way.
Lay a damp cloth, so the wet fibres hold the marble.
Make the lane from several different strips, with the softest one last.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own escape lane. Draw it, build it and test it 3 times. What was the mean stopping distance? Which idea from real roads does your lane use?

setup.art: The cardboard ramp from the Stopping Distance Test with a marble held at the top mark, and a ruler marking a line 20 centimetres beyond the end of the channel.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a line 20 centimetres from the end of the channel.

setup.art: A large tray of uncooked rice with the end of the cardboard channel resting inside it, and a marble sunk a little way into the rice close to the channel.
setup.caption: 2. Build a lane that stops the marble before the line.

flow.do: 1. Set up the ramp as in the Stopping Distance Test, with a bedsheet at the bottom. 2. Roll the marble from the 30 centimetre mark 3 times. 3. Find the mean distance. 4. Mark a line 20 centimetres from the end of the channel.
flow.say: First we need the number to beat. How far does the marble roll on the bedsheet from the top mark?
flow.kid: Roll the marble from the top mark 3 times. Find the mean. Mark a line at 20 cm.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Escape Lane. Here you measure how far the marble rolls on a bedsheet.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a folded towel, a doormat, a blanket. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Test it 3 times and find the mean.
flow.say: Which surface do you think will take the marble's energy away fastest? Why? Let's test your choice 3 times.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Test it 3 times. Find the mean.

ask.q: Why does a soft, thick surface stop the marble sooner?
good: The marble sinks in and has to squash the surface as it rolls.
The force against the marble is bigger, so its energy is used up in a shorter distance.

flow.context: This step of the Escape Lane tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a lane of their own and draws it. 2. They build it and test it 3 times. 3. They compare the mean with the 20 centimetre line and with the bedsheet.
flow.say: Now design your own lane. What will you change, and why? Did it stop the marble before the line?
flow.kid: Design your own lane. Draw it. Build it. Test it 3 times. Did the marble stop in time?
flow.parent: A tray of rice usually stops the marble within a few centimetres. The marble must stop before the far rim, or the rim counts as a wall. Wash the rice before cooking it.

check.q: A bed of loose gravel stops a runaway lorry in a short distance. Why?
options: The gravel pushes against the wheels with a very big force
The gravel makes the lorry lighter
The gravel cools the brakes
check.why: The wheels sink into the loose gravel and must push it aside. That is a very big force against the movement. So the lorry's kinetic energy is used up in a short distance.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Escape Lane. Here you build and test your own design.

challenges.title: The Cool Coin: 80 strokes with the least heat
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Warm Coin Test, a coin rubbed for 80 firm strokes on cardboard became hot. Here you must do the same 80 strokes and keep the coin as cool as you can.
challenges.problem: Rub a coin for 80 firm strokes between two lines 20 centimetres apart. Change the surface, or put something on it, so that the coin ends as cool as possible.
constraints: Do all 80 strokes, at the same speed and with the same firm press as in the Warm Coin Test.
Use the same kind of coin, and start with a cool one.
A judge with closed eyes gives the warmth score from 0 to 3.
general: Put a drop of oil on the cardboard.
Dust the cardboard with talcum powder.
Rub the cardboard with candle wax first.

Rub on a damp cloth, so that the water takes up the heat.
Use both ideas together: a lubricant to make less heat, and metal or water to carry the heat away.

good: It makes the friction force smaller.
A smaller force over the same distance turns less energy into heat.

check.q: Engine oil keeps the moving parts of an engine cooler. What are the two ways it does this?
options: It makes friction smaller, and it carries heat away
It makes friction bigger, and it traps heat
It makes the parts lighter, and it stops them moving
check.why: Oil between the parts makes the friction force smaller, so less heat is made. The oil also flows, and it carries heat away from the hottest parts.
