items.p: What must be true before friction can act between two things?
items.why: Friction is a contact force, so the two surfaces must touch. Choosing 'moving' forgets static friction, which acts on things that are still.

items.p: True or false: friction can act on a thing that is not moving.
items.why: True. Static friction holds a book still on a tilted board. A strong answer gives an example like this.

items.p: Friction acts against ____ between two surfaces that touch.
items.why: Friction acts against sliding, or against the sliding that would happen without it. 'Movement' is close, but friction can also push a thing the way it moves.

items.p: Sort these forces into contact forces and non-contact forces.
items.why: Friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust act only on things that touch a surface, air or water. Gravity and a magnet's force act across a gap.
items: a magnet's force on a pin

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: friction that pushes a walker or a wheel forward
something slippery that makes friction smaller
the force from air or water against a moving thing
the slow loss of material from a rubbing surface
friction between surfaces that are not sliding

items.p: Draw a book sliding to the right across a table. Add the friction arrow and label it.
items.a: A box on a line, with an arrow along the table pointing to the left, labelled 'friction'.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the arrow along the table top, pointing against the slide. An arrow pointing down or to the right shows a mix-up with gravity or with the push.
items.art: A blank table top with a book on it and a small arrow above the book showing that it moves to the right.

items.p: In the Stopping Distance Test, the marble stopped sooner on a towel than on a bedsheet. What does that show?
opts: The towel pushed back with a bigger force
The marble was slower on the towel's ramp
The bedsheet made the marble heavier
items.why: The marble had the same energy at the bottom each time. The towel used that energy up in a shorter distance, so its force against the marble was bigger.

items.p: On a bicycle, sort these places into friction we want and friction we do not want.
items.why: We want grip at the tyres, brake pads, pedals and handle grips. We want easy sliding in the axles and the chain, so those are oiled.

items.p: True or false: a drop of oil on a hinge makes the friction there bigger.
items.why: False. Oil is a lubricant. The metal parts slide on a thin layer of oil, so the friction is smaller and the squeak stops.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair stopping distance test in order.
a: Build the ramp and mark the start places
Guess what will happen and say why
Roll the marble 3 times on each surface
Find the mean for each surface and draw a chart
items.why: First set up, then predict, then test with repeats, then work out the results.
items: Roll the marble 3 times on each surface
Find the mean for each surface and draw a chart
Build the ramp and mark the start places
Guess what will happen and say why

items.p: In Finger Walk, loose paper slid backward when two fingers walked forward on it. Explain why.
items.a: The fingers push backward on the paper. The paper is loose, so it slides backward. When the paper is held still, friction from the paper pushes the fingers forward.
items.why: A strong answer says which way the fingers push, and that friction on the fingers points the other way, forward.

items.p: When friction stops a sliding thing, its kinetic energy turns into ____.
items.why: Friction turns kinetic energy into thermal energy, which we call heat. The energy is not destroyed.

items.p: Three of these make friction smaller. Which one makes it bigger?
items.why: Oil, ball bearings and polish all make friction smaller. Tread on a tyre helps the rubber grip a wet road, so it is there for more friction.

items.p: On a drawing of a bicycle, label two places where friction is wanted and two where it is not.
a: Wanted: brake pads on the rim
items.why: Pedals, handle grips and the seat are also right for 'wanted'. The pedal axle and the brake cable are also right for 'not wanted'.
items.art: A side view of a bicycle with four blank label lines.

items.p: Why do your palms get warm when you rub them together?
opts: Friction turns the movement into heat
Rubbing squeezes blood into the palms
The air between them catches fire
Skin stores heat until it is rubbed
items.why: Your arm muscles give the hands kinetic energy, and friction between the palms turns it into heat. Nothing was stored in the skin beforehand.

items.p: A box rides on a lorry that is speeding up. Which way does friction push the box?
items.why: Without friction the box would be left behind and slide backward. Friction acts against that slide, so it points forward and speeds the box up.

items.p: In the Riding Katori, a katori moved when the cloth under it was pulled slowly. Which force moved it? Explain.
items.a: Friction from the cloth moved the katori. Only the cloth touched the katori. Without friction the cloth would slide out from under it, so friction pushed the katori the way the cloth moved.
items.why: A strong answer says that only the cloth touched the katori, and that friction acted against sliding between the two.

items.p: True or false: a book resting on a tilted board has no friction on it.
items.why: False. Without friction the book would slide down. Static friction points up the slope and holds the book still.

items.p: Three runs of a marble on a towel are 22, 26 and 24 centimetres. What is the mean, in centimetres?
items.why: 22 + 26 + 24 = 72. Then 72 ÷ 3 = 24. The mean is 24 centimetres.

items.p: A marble starts twice as high on the same ramp and towel. About how far does it roll?
items.why: Twice the height gives about twice the kinetic energy at the bottom. The towel takes away about the same energy in each centimetre, so the marble rolls about twice as far.

items.p: Draw a walker's back foot as she steps forward. Show the foot's push and the friction on the foot.
items.a: A foot on a floor line. One arrow on the floor pointing backward, labelled 'foot pushes floor'. One arrow on the foot pointing forward, labelled 'friction on foot'.
items.why: A strong drawing has two arrows of the same length pointing opposite ways. The friction arrow is on the foot and points forward.
items.art: A blank floor line with the outline of a foot about to push off.

items.p: Three people talk about friction on a bicycle.
items.a: A strong answer names places on the cycle for each side: axles and chain for the racer, brake pads and tyres for the brake maker, wear for the mechanic. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: All three are right about a different part of the cycle. The same force helps in one place and costs effort or parts in another.

views.says: Friction is my enemy. It takes my effort and turns it into heat.
Friction is what keeps a rider alive. Without it nobody could stop or turn.
Friction is neither. But it wears out every part, and somebody has to pay for new ones.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use two parts of a bicycle as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: Mean stopping distances for one marble are listed. Put the surfaces in order, from most friction to least.
items.why: The marble had the same energy each time. A shorter stopping distance means a bigger force against the marble.

items.p: A cycle at twice the speed has ____ times the kinetic energy.
items.why: Kinetic energy grows with the speed multiplied by itself. Two times two is four. That is why braking distance grows so fast with speed.

items.p: Match each trouble at home to a fix that makes sense.
items.why: Oil and wax are lubricants, for less friction. Rubber and a damp cloth grip, for more friction. Rollers swap sliding for rolling.
pairs: A jar lid that slips in the hand
a rubber band round the lid
A heavy trunk to move across a room

items.p: In the Warm Coin Test, a firm press warmed the coin more than a light press. Why?
opts: The cardboard was hotter to begin with
items.why: A firmer press makes a bigger friction force. Energy turned into heat is force multiplied by distance, so the same strokes make more heat.

items.p: Three of these forces act against a movement. Which one does not?
items.why: Sliding friction, air resistance and water resistance all act against movement. Upthrust pushes upward on a thing in water or air, even when the thing is still.

items.p: Label the forces on a marble rolling to the right across a towel.
a: Rolling resistance (friction): pointing to the left
Direction of movement: to the right
items.why: Gravity and the floor's push are balanced, so the marble does not move up or down. Only the force against the rolling is left, so the marble slows.
items.art: A marble on a towel with an arrow above it pointing right and three blank label lines.

items.p: A swimmer dives with her hands together and her body straight. Explain why, using water resistance.
items.a: Water resistance depends on the shape and on how big a front pushes through the water. Hands together and a straight body make a narrow, streamlined shape. So the water resistance is smaller and she keeps her speed.
items.why: A strong answer uses the words 'water resistance' or 'drag', and links a narrow front to a smaller force.

items.p: True or false: when friction stops a cycle, the cycle's kinetic energy is destroyed.
items.why: False. Energy is never destroyed. The kinetic energy becomes heat in the brake pads, the rims, the tyres and the road.

items.p: Many books say friction always acts against a thing's movement. Give one example that fits and one that does not.
items.a: Fits: a sliding carrom coin, a braking cycle or a rolling ball. Does not fit: a walker's foot, a wheel that drives a car, or a katori carried on a moving cloth. In those, friction points the way the thing moves.
items.why: A strong answer gives one of each, and then states the full rule: friction acts against sliding between the two surfaces.

items.p: Two tyre makers disagree about the best tyre for a school bus in Kochi.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are right in different weather. A smooth tyre puts the most rubber on a dry road. Tread lets water escape, so rubber still touches a wet road. For Kochi's long monsoon it chooses tread, and it grants the first maker's point about dry roads.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Racing cars use smooth tyres on dry tracks and change to treaded tyres in rain.

views.says: A smooth tyre is best. It puts the most rubber on the road, so it grips most.
A tyre with deep tread is best. The grooves let rainwater escape, so the rubber still touches the road.

items.ask: Which tyre would you choose for a school bus in Kochi, and why? Then say when the other maker would be right.

items.p: A car at 30 kilometres an hour stops in 6 metres. About how far does it need at 60?
items.why: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy. The same braking force needs four times the distance: 4 × 6 = 24 metres. Choosing 12 metres means doubling the distance with the speed.

items.p: Plan a fair test of this question: does a wet cloth stop a rolling marble sooner than a dry cloth?
items.a: Change only one thing: whether the cloth is dry or wet. Measure the stopping distance. Keep the same marble, ramp, start mark and kind of cloth. Roll 3 times on each and find the mean.
items.why: A strong answer names what to change, what to measure and what to keep the same. It also repeats each run.

items.p: True or false: a suitcase riding on a level belt at a steady speed needs friction to keep it going.
items.why: False. The suitcase and the belt move together at a steady speed, so nothing is trying to slide. Friction is needed only when the belt speeds up, slows down or turns.

items.p: A cycle brakes with a friction force of 40 newtons and stops in 5 metres. How many joules become heat?
items.why: Energy turned into heat is force multiplied by distance. 40 × 5 = 200 joules.

items.p: A train's wheels spin on wet rails. Why does the loco pilot lower the power before using sand?
opts: Sand works only on a cold rail
Less power makes the train lighter
items.why: Sliding friction is smaller than the biggest static friction. So a wheel that spins grips less than one that holds. Lowering the power lets the wheel stop slipping, and the sand then adds grip.

items.p: A wheel that grips the road and pushes a car forward is using ____.
items.why: Traction is friction that pushes a wheel or a walker forward.

items.p: Sort each one by the force that mainly slows it: friction between solids, or drag from air or water.
items.why: Brake pads, a carrom coin and rubbed palms are solids sliding on solids. A parachute, a ship and a diving bird are slowed by air or water.
items: a cycle with its brakes on
a ship after the engine stops
a kingfisher diving into a pond
one palm rubbed on the other

items.p: A box rides on a lorry speeding up to the right. Draw friction on the box and on the floor.
items.a: On the box: an arrow pointing right, labelled 'friction on box'. On the lorry's floor: an arrow of the same length pointing left, labelled 'friction on floor'.
items.why: Friction comes as a pair. The floor pushes the box forward, and the box pushes the floor backward just as hard.
items.art: A side view of a flat-backed lorry with a box on it and an arrow showing that the lorry speeds up to the right.

items.p: A cyclist pedals up to speed and then brakes. Put the energy changes in order.
a: Energy from food is stored in her muscles
Her muscles turn it into the kinetic energy of the cycle
The brakes turn the kinetic energy into heat in the pads and rims
The heat spreads into the air
items.why: Energy is never lost. It changes form at each step, and the last form is heat spread through the air.
items: The brakes turn the kinetic energy into heat in the pads and rims
Energy from food is stored in her muscles
The heat spreads into the air
Her muscles turn it into the kinetic energy of the cycle

items.p: In the Warm Coin Test, the judge kept their eyes closed. Why does that make the result more trustworthy?
items.a: A judge who knows a coin was rubbed 80 times expects it to be hot. That judge may give a higher score. With closed eyes the judge can use only what the skin feels. So the scores come from the coin and not from the judge's guess.
items.why: A strong answer says that expecting a result can change what a person reports. Hiding the treatment removes this.

items.p: Match each scene to the kind of friction or drag in it.
items.why: Each scene has surfaces that hold, slide or roll, or a thing moving through air or water.
pairs: A pen held between the fingers
A carrom coin crossing the board
A marble rolling on a towel
A kite pulled along by the wind
A fish swimming in a pond

items.p: Three of these changes make a rubbed coin warmer. Which one keeps it cooler?
items.why: More strokes, longer strokes and a firmer press all raise the force or the distance, so more energy becomes heat. Oil makes the friction force smaller.

items.p: Lorries use a low gear on a long downhill ghat road. Explain why, using friction and heat.
items.a: Going downhill, a lorry would keep gaining kinetic energy. Brakes turn that energy into heat by friction. On a long slope the brakes get so hot that they stop gripping well. In a low gear the engine holds the lorry back, so the brakes do less and stay cooler.
items.why: A strong answer says where the heat comes from, and why too much heat in the brakes is dangerous.

quiz.p: Which of these is a contact force?
opts: A magnet's force on a pin
The Earth's pull on the Moon
quiz.why: Friction acts only where two surfaces touch. The other three act across a gap, so they are non-contact forces.

quiz.p: A carrom coin slides to the right. Which way does friction push the coin?
quiz.why: The coin slides to the right over the board. Friction acts against that slide, so it points to the left.

quiz.p: You start to walk forward. Which way does friction from the floor push your back foot?
quiz.why: Your foot pushes backward on the floor and would slide backward without friction. So friction on the foot points forward. Choosing 'backward' means using the rule 'friction is against movement', which is only half right.

quiz.p: A train's wheels spin on wet rails, and the train stays still. What is missing?
opts: Enough friction between wheels and rails
quiz.why: The engine is turning the wheels, so power is not the problem. The rails must push the wheels forward by friction, and wet rails give too little.

quiz.p: In a stopping distance test, why do you roll the marble three times on each surface?
opts: One run can be a fluke
The marble needs to warm up
quiz.why: A small push or a wrinkle can spoil one run. Three runs and a mean give a number you can trust more.

quiz.p: Which pair names useful friction first, and unwanted friction second, on a bicycle?
quiz.why: Brake pads must grip the rim, so friction there is useful. An axle must turn easily, so friction there wastes the rider's effort.

quiz.p: One coin is rubbed for 80 strokes and another for 20, in the same way. Which is warmer, and why?
opts: The 80-stroke coin: longer rubbing, more heat
The 20-stroke coin: less time to cool
Both the same: friction force was equal
quiz.why: Energy turned into heat is friction force multiplied by distance rubbed. Four times the strokes is four times the distance, so more heat.

quiz.p: After a rolling ball stops, where has its kinetic energy gone?
opts: Into heat in the ball, floor and air
Back into the hand that rolled it
quiz.why: Friction and air resistance turn kinetic energy into heat. The heat spreads out, so we do not notice it, but the energy still exists.

quiz.p: A cycle goes twice as fast and brakes in the same way. About how far does it need to stop?
quiz.why: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy. The same braking force needs four times the distance to turn it all into heat.

quiz.p: Which force from water acts on a boat even when the boat is still?
quiz.why: Upthrust pushes up on anything in water, moving or still. Water resistance acts only when the boat moves through the water.

quiz.p: Which of these is still not fully understood by scientists?
opts: Exactly how sliding atoms turn movement into heat
quiz.why: Scientists agree that friction makes heat, that oil lowers friction and that friction is a contact force. The exact steps by which sliding atoms pass on their energy are still being studied.

applications: Brakes on cycles, autos, cars and trains press a pad against a turning rim, disc or wheel. Friction turns the vehicle's kinetic energy into heat.
Railway engines are made heavy and carry sand. The rails can push a train forward only through friction with the wheels.
The grooves in a tyre let rainwater escape, so that rubber still touches the road in the monsoon.
Ball bearings and oil cut the unwanted friction in ceiling fans, mixers, cycles and engines. About one fifth of the world's energy is used up overcoming friction.
Metro trains and electric cars use regenerative braking. The motors slow the wheels and turn part of the kinetic energy back into electricity.
Fast trains, racing cycles and swimmers' caps are streamlined, to make air resistance or water resistance smaller.
A wet grinder crushes soaked rice and urad dal for idli batter by friction between heavy stones. The batter comes out slightly warm.

open_questions.q: At the level of atoms, how exactly does sliding turn into heat?
open_questions.why_open: The energy goes into shaking atoms, and some goes into electrons. The shares have been measured only for a few special materials.

open_questions.q: What happens in the instant when a still thing starts to slide?
open_questions.why_open: Fast cameras show tiny cracks racing along the touching surfaces just before sliding starts. Nobody can yet predict them for everyday surfaces.

open_questions.q: How much harm does the dust from tyres and brakes do?
open_questions.why_open: Tyre dust is one of the largest sources of tiny plastic pieces in rivers and seas. Its effect on fish, people and other animals is still being measured.

open_questions.q: Why do faults in the Earth become so slippery during an earthquake?
open_questions.why_open: In laboratory tests, rock sliding fast loses most of its friction, perhaps because friction heats the rock. Nobody can watch a real fault deep underground.

open_questions.q: How much of the energy lost to friction can the world save?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers think better surfaces and oils could save a large share. How fast that can happen in real engines and factories is not known.

maths.problem: In the Stopping Distance Test, three runs on a bedsheet were 92, 100 and 96 centimetres. What is the mean?
maths.explain: Add the three runs: 92 + 100 + 96 = 288. Divide by the number of runs: 288 ÷ 3 = 96. So the mean is 96 centimetres.
maths.context: This is about the Stopping Distance Test. A marble rolls off a ramp onto a cloth, and you measure how far it goes.

chart.title: Made-up example: three runs on a bedsheet

maths.why_maths: One run can be a fluke. The mean of three runs is a number you can trust more.

maths.problem: The marble's mean stopping distance was 24 centimetres on a towel and 96 centimetres on a bedsheet. How many times as far did it roll on the bedsheet? What does that say about the two forces?
maths.answer: 4 times as far. The force from the towel was about 4 times as big.
maths.explain: 96 ÷ 24 = 4. The marble had the same energy at the bottom both times. The towel used up that energy in a quarter of the distance. Energy is force multiplied by distance, so the towel's force was about 4 times as big.
maths.context: This is about the Stopping Distance Test. A marble rolls from the same mark onto a towel and then onto a bedsheet.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one distance by the other shows how many times further the marble went. That tells us how the forces compare.

maths.problem: On a towel, the marble's mean stopping distances were 12, 24 and 36 centimetres. The start marks were 10, 20 and 30 centimetres. What do you expect from a 40 centimetre mark on a longer ramp?
maths.explain: Each extra 10 centimetres of start adds 12 centimetres of rolling. The pattern is 12, 24, 36, so the next number is 48. Real results will be close to this, not exact.
maths.context: This is about part 2 of the Stopping Distance Test, where the marble starts from three marks on the ramp.

chart.title: Made-up example: stopping distance on a towel

maths.why_maths: A pattern in the results lets you predict a test you have not done yet. Then you can check the prediction.

maths.problem: A cyclist brakes. The friction force on the wheels is 50 newtons, and the cycle stops in 8 metres. How many joules of kinetic energy turned into heat?
maths.explain: Energy turned into heat is the friction force multiplied by the distance. 50 × 8 = 400. One joule is the energy used when a force of 1 newton acts through 1 metre.
maths.context: In the Warm Coin Test, a bigger force and a longer rub both made more heat. This problem works out how much heat a brake makes.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying force by distance gives the amount of heat as a number. Then two brakes or two rubs can be compared.

maths.problem: A cycle at 10 kilometres an hour stops in 2 metres with the brakes on hard. Twice the speed means 4 times the kinetic energy, and 3 times the speed means 9 times. How far does the cycle need at 20 and at 30 kilometres an hour?
maths.answer: About 8 metres at 20 kilometres an hour, and about 18 metres at 30.
maths.explain: The brakes give the same force, so the distance grows with the energy. At 20: 4 × 2 = 8 metres. At 30: 9 × 2 = 18 metres. Three times the speed needs nine times the distance.
maths.context: In the Stopping Distance Test, a marble with twice the energy rolled about twice as far. This problem uses the same idea for a cycle that brakes.
maths.why_maths: The numbers show why a little more speed needs a lot more road to stop.

maths.problem: Four runs of a marble on a towel were 23, 25, 24 and 61 centimetres. Which run looks wrong? What is the mean of the other three? What should you do about the odd run?
maths.answer: The 61 centimetre run looks wrong. The mean of the other three is 24 centimetres. Roll that run again and write down what happened.
maths.explain: Three runs are within 2 centimetres of each other, and 61 is far away. Perhaps the marble got a push, or missed the towel. 23 + 25 + 24 = 72, and 72 ÷ 3 = 24. If 61 were included, the mean would be about 33, which matches none of the runs.
maths.context: This is about the Stopping Distance Test, where each run is repeated because one run can be a fluke.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the spread of the numbers before finding a mean shows up a run that went wrong.

quiz: Friction can act on a thing that is standing still.
Static friction holds a book still on a tilted board.
Friction always pushes against the way a thing moves.
Friction pushes a walker's foot forward, the way she moves.
Gravity is a contact force.
Gravity acts across a gap, so it is a non-contact force.
Rubbing a coin for more strokes makes more heat.
A longer rub turns more kinetic energy into heat.
Oil makes friction bigger.
Oil is a lubricant, so it makes friction smaller.
A train moves forward because of friction from the rails.
The wheels push back on the rails, and the rails push the train forward.
Upthrust is a kind of friction.
Upthrust pushes up on a thing in water or air, even when the thing is still.
A cycle at twice the speed needs about twice the distance to brake.
It needs about four times the distance, because it has four times the kinetic energy.
Air resistance grows when you go faster.
Drag from air and water grows quickly with speed.
The energy that friction takes from a moving thing is destroyed.
The energy becomes heat. Energy is never destroyed.
odd: Friction, air resistance and upthrust are contact forces, but gravity acts across a gap.
Oil, grease and powder make friction smaller, but tread helps a tyre grip.
We want friction at brake pads, tyres and soles, but not in an axle.
Friction pushes the coin, the cycle and the ball backward, but it pushes the walker's foot forward.
Friction heats brakes, a match and rubbed palms, but an ice cube melts from the room's warmth.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that friction can move a train? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Two hundred years ago, many engineers believed that a smooth iron wheel could never grip a smooth iron rail. They thought an engine pulling heavy wagons would only spin its wheels. So in 1811 John Blenkinsop patented a rail with teeth along one side. He worked at a coal mine near Leeds in England. His engines, built by Matthew Murray, pulled themselves along with a toothed wheel. Around 1812 William Hedley, a manager at Wylam coal mine, decided to test the belief. He built a test carriage that men drove by hand. He loaded it with weights and hooked coal wagons behind it. With little weight on it, the wheels spun. With more weight pressing the wheels onto the rails, the smooth wheels gripped and pulled the wagons. The friction had grown with the weight. In 1813 Hedley, with Timothy Hackworth and Jonathan Forster, built Puffing Billy, a steam engine with smooth wheels. Puffing Billy now stands in the Science Museum in London. Almost every train in the world runs on smooth wheels.
how_we_found_out.who: John Blenkinsop and Matthew Murray, who built the toothed railway. William Hedley, Timothy Hackworth and Jonathan Forster, who built Puffing Billy at Wylam.
how_we_found_out.when: 1811 (Blenkinsop's toothed rail), about 1812 (Hedley's test carriage) and 1813 (Puffing Billy)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That smooth iron wheels cannot grip smooth iron rails well enough to pull a heavy load. Hedley's loaded test carriage showed that they can, if enough weight presses the wheels down.
how_we_found_out.art: A small early steam engine with smooth wheels pulling coal wagons on plain rails, beside a rail with teeth and a toothed wheel crossed out.

roots.context: We have learned that friction is a contact force that acts against sliding, and that it turns movement into heat. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Finger Walk, your fingers walked forward and the loose paper slid backward. Your fingers pushed the paper back, so friction pushed your fingers forward. In the Stopping Distance Test, friction slowed the marble until it was as still as the towel. In both cases, friction pushed the two touching surfaces towards moving together at the same speed. Sometimes that meant starting to move, and sometimes it meant stopping.
deep_truth.habit: We call friction 'the force that slows things down'. But friction does not always point backward. It always acts against sliding between two surfaces. So it slows some things down and speeds other things up.
deep_truth.evidence: In Finger Walk, loose paper slid backward under walking fingers. In the Riding Katori, a steel bowl on a cloth began to move when the cloth was pulled. Nothing else touched the bowl. In the Stopping Distance Test, a rolling marble came to rest on a towel.

three.who_am_i: Every step you take is a push from the ground. You move through the world by pushing on it and being pushed back.
three.what_is_life: Every animal that walks, crawls or climbs moves by friction. A snake's belly scales grip the ground, and the ground pushes her forward.
three.what_is_this_world: Friction is never a property of one thing alone. It exists only where two surfaces meet. It pushes on both surfaces with equal strength.

roots.thread: Friction is one force, but we notice it in many ways. We feel it as the grip of a shoe, the squeal of a brake and the warmth of rubbed hands. We see it in the thin heel of an old chappal. All of these have the same cause. The atoms of two touching surfaces hold on to each other with electric forces. Depending on what the surfaces are doing, that holding shows up as grip, as heat or as wear.

teachings.teaching: Difficult and easy complete each other. Long and short shape each other. Before and after follow each other.
teachings.link: We call friction useful on a brake and unwanted in an axle, yet the force is the same. 'Useful' and 'unwanted' describe what we want at that moment. Each word has meaning only beside the other.

teachings.teaching: Whatever arises by depending on other things has no existence of its own, apart from them.
teachings.link: A chappal has no friction by itself, and neither has a floor. Friction arises only when the two meet, and it changes when either one changes.

science.text: Every force comes as a pair. When one surface pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard (Newton's third law, 1687).
Energy is never destroyed. Work done against friction turns into the same amount of heat (James Joule, 1840s).
How sliding atoms pass their movement on as heat is still being worked out in detail.

other_view.view: Friction has no aim. It is the sum of countless tiny electric forces between the atoms of two surfaces. Saying that friction 'works to' make surfaces move together is only our way of describing how the sums come out.

practice.title: Feel the floor push you
practice.say: Stand with bare feet on the floor. Let's close our eyes and feel the soles of our feet. Now lean forward very slowly, as if you were about to take a step. Feel your toes press backward against the floor. The floor is pushing you forward just as hard. Now open your eyes. Take five slow steps, and notice the floor's push in every one.
practice.kid: Stand in bare feet. Close your eyes. Lean forward slowly. Feel your toes press back on the floor. The floor pushes you forward. Open your eyes. Take five slow steps.

ask: Friction pushes you forward at every step. So when you walk, who is moving you: you, or the floor?
The same friction is useful in a brake and unwanted in an axle. Is 'useful' in the friction, or in what we want?
Friction exists only where two surfaces meet. Is there anything about you that exists only when you meet someone or something else?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home. Please treat the amounts as a starting point. The Stopping Distance Test (core) needs a marble, a cardboard strip, books, a bath towel and a bedsheet. How far the marble rolls depends on the cloth. So the trial run tells you to add or take away a book before you measure. Expect about double the distance from double the start mark, not exactly double. On a bare floor the marble may reach the wall. The Warm Coin Test (core) needs two people, three coins of one kind and thick cardboard. In a cold room 20 strokes may feel like nothing. The step says to rub faster, press harder or double every number. A coin after 80 firm strokes can sting, so touch it for one second only. Finger Walk needs a smooth table or a steel tray. On a rough wooden table the paper may not slide. The Riding Katori needs an empty katori, because a tall tumbler can tip over on the fast pull. Hand in the Bucket wets the floor, so do it in the bathroom. Only a grown-up strikes the match in Pencil, Eraser, Match. In the Escape Lane, the tray of rice must be large, so that the marble stops before the far rim. Shove Coin leaves powder on the table, and a powdered floor is slippery, so wipe it up. Green and Red is written for a bicycle, with a door and chappals as the other choice. The Home Friction Service needs a grown-up for the oil. No part needs a garden. Hedley's test is now dated 'about 1812', the Delhi Metro date and the 'steepest' claim were removed, and the engine count in the story is marked as imagined. Four thousand horsepower is a round figure. Four times the braking distance at twice the speed leaves out the driver's reaction distance. The Tao Te Ching and Nagarjuna lines are paraphrases.
